title: Programming & Scripting
intro: Code turns a security professional from a tool user into a problem solver. You will learn Python, Bash, PowerShell, JavaScript and SQL with a defensive, automation-first mindset.
objectives: Write Python scripts with functions, files, JSON and regex
Automate tasks in Bash and PowerShell
Understand JavaScript and browser security basics
Query databases with SQL and prevent SQL injection
Build safe defensive automation

lessons.title: Python Fundamentals: Types, Collections, Conditions and Loops
lessons.why: Python is the most widely used language in security tooling, automation and data analysis.
objectives: Use variables, strings and numbers
Store data in lists, tuples, dictionaries and sets
Control flow with if, for and while
lessons.simple: Python is a readable programming language. A variable stores a value: port = 443. Data types include int (whole numbers), float (decimals), str (text), bool (True/False). Collections hold many values: a list [22, 80, 443] is ordered and changeable, a tuple (10, 20) cannot change, a dict {"ssh": 22} maps keys to values, and a set {"admin", "guest"} holds unique items. if/elif/else make decisions; for and while loops repeat work.
lessons.analogy: Variables are labelled boxes; a list is a row of boxes; a dictionary is a filing cabinet with labelled drawers.
lessons.example: A SOC analyst uses a set to de-duplicate 50,000 IP addresses from logs down to 312 unique sources in one line.
lessons.relevance: Every later security script - log parsers, report generators, API clients - is built from these basics.
practice: Create a dict of five services and their ports and print them
Write a loop that prints only even numbers 1-20
Use a set to remove duplicates from a list of IPs
lessons.challenge: Write a script that takes a list of usernames and prints any that appear more than once.
mistakes: Wrong indentation
Modifying a list while looping over it
Using == to compare to None instead of 'is None'
lessons.summary: Variables, types, collections, conditions and loops are the building blocks of every script.
lessons.examTip: Know which collection is ordered, which is immutable and which removes duplicates.

quiz.q: Which Python type maps keys to values?
Which collection automatically removes duplicates?
What defines a code block in Python?
quiz.explain: Indentation is part of Python syntax.

lessons.title: Python Functions, Modules, Classes, Files, Errors, JSON, CSV and Regex
lessons.why: Real tools read files, parse formats and handle errors gracefully.
objectives: Write reusable functions and import modules
Read and write files, JSON and CSV
Handle exceptions and use regular expressions
lessons.simple: Functions package reusable logic: def is_private(ip): ... return True. Modules are files of code you import, like import json or import re. Classes bundle data and behaviour into objects. Files are opened with 'with open("log.txt") as f:' which closes them automatically. Exceptions are errors you can catch with try/except so a script does not crash. JSON and CSV are common data formats, and regular expressions (regex) find patterns such as IP addresses in text.
lessons.analogy: A function is a recipe you can reuse; a module is a recipe book; exceptions are the fire blanket you keep ready in case something goes wrong.
lessons.example: Incident responders write small Python parsers to turn messy firewall exports into JSON that can be loaded into a dashboard.
lessons.relevance: Parsing logs, normalising data and handling bad input safely are everyday security engineering tasks.
practice: Write a function that returns True if a password is at least 12 characters
Load a CSV of assets and print those marked 'critical'
Write a regex that matches an email address
lessons.challenge: Build a Finding class with title, severity and remediation, then export a list of findings to JSON.
mistakes: Bare 'except:' that hides real errors
Forgetting encoding when reading files
Using subprocess with shell=True on untrusted input
lessons.summary: Functions, modules and classes organise code; with-blocks handle files; try/except handles errors; JSON, CSV and regex process data.
lessons.examTip: Exam tasks often ask you to spot a bug - check indentation, exception handling and file closing.

quiz.q: Why use 'with open(...) as f'?
quiz.explain: The context manager guarantees the file is closed.

quiz.q: Which module parses JSON?
What is risky about subprocess with shell=True and user input?
quiz.explain: Untrusted input can inject extra shell commands.

lessons.title: Python for Security: HTTP, APIs, Automation, Logging, Testing and Secure Coding
lessons.why: Most modern security work touches APIs. Secure coding stops you creating the vulnerabilities you will later learn to find.
objectives: Make HTTP requests and call APIs
Log and test your scripts
Apply secure coding principles
lessons.simple: HTTP is how programs talk to web servers. In Python you can use the built-in urllib or the popular requests library to send GET and POST requests and read JSON responses from APIs. Good scripts log what they do (the logging module) and are tested (unittest or pytest). Secure coding means validating input, never hardcoding secrets, handling errors without leaking details, and using safe libraries.
lessons.detailed:
Example - query a lab API with a timeout and API key from the environment:

import os, requests, logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
API = "http://api.lab.local/v1/assets"
key = os.environ.get("LAB_API_KEY")   # never hardcode secrets
resp = requests.get(API, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}"}, timeout=10)
resp.raise_for_status()
for asset in resp.json():
    logging.info("Asset %s owner=%s", asset["name"], asset["owner"])

Status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 301/302 redirect, 400 bad request, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 429 too many requests, 500 server error.

Testing: def test_is_private(): assert is_private("10.0.0.1"). Run with pytest.

Secure coding checklist: validate and whitelist input; parameterise database queries; encode output; least privilege; secrets in environment variables or a vault; pin and update dependencies; set timeouts; handle exceptions without printing stack traces to users; log security events but never log passwords or tokens.

Automation ethics: only send requests to systems you are authorised to test, respect rate limits and never automate attacks against third parties.
lessons.analogy: An API is a restaurant menu for programs: you order (request) in a defined format and the kitchen returns a dish (response).
lessons.example: A team automated their weekly vulnerability export with a 40-line Python script calling their scanner's API - saving four hours of manual work each week.
lessons.relevance: APIs are both an attack surface and an automation tool. Secure coding knowledge is required for AppSec and DevSecOps roles.
practice: Write a function that returns a description for an HTTP status code
Add logging to a previous script
Write two pytest tests for is_private()
lessons.challenge: Review a script that has an API key hardcoded on line 3 and rewrite it securely.
mistakes: Hardcoding API keys in code or Git
No timeouts on network requests
Logging full request bodies containing passwords
lessons.summary: Use HTTP and APIs carefully, log and test everything, keep secrets out of code and validate all input.
lessons.examTip: Know 401 vs 403: 401 = not authenticated, 403 = authenticated but not allowed.

quiz.q: Which status code means 'authenticated but not allowed'?
Where should an API key for a script be stored?
options: In an environment variable or secrets vault

quiz.q: Network requests in scripts should set a timeout.
quiz.explain: Without a timeout a script can hang forever.

lessons.title: Bash and PowerShell Scripting
lessons.why: Shell scripts glue tools together on servers and endpoints - fast wins for audits and administration.
objectives: Write Bash scripts with variables, conditions, loops and functions
Write PowerShell scripts using objects and pipelines
Automate safe system audits
lessons.simple: A Bash script is a text file of shell commands starting with #!/bin/bash. It can use variables (NAME="lab"), conditions (if [ -f file ]; then ... fi), loops (for f in *.log; do ... done) and functions. PowerShell scripts (.ps1) use cmdlets that pass objects, not plain text, through pipelines, which makes filtering and sorting powerful: Get-Service | Where-Object Status -eq 'Running' | Sort-Object Name.
lessons.detailed:
Bash audit example:

#!/bin/bash
# quick-audit.sh - read-only checks for your own lab VM
echo "== Listening ports =="; ss -tulpn
echo "== SUID files =="; find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
echo "== Users with shells =="; grep -E "bash|zsh" /etc/passwd | cut -d: -f1
if grep -q "^PermitRootLogin yes" /etc/ssh/sshd_config; then
  echo "WARNING: root SSH login allowed"
fi

Key Bash features: $1 (first argument), $? (last exit code), $(command) (command substitution), read (input), set -euo pipefail (safer scripts), quoting variables "$var" to avoid word splitting.

PowerShell audit example:

$admins = Get-LocalGroupMember -Group Administrators
$fw = Get-NetFirewallProfile | Select-Object Name, Enabled
$report = [PSCustomObject]@{ Host=$env:COMPUTERNAME; Admins=$admins.Count; Firewall=$fw }
$report | ConvertTo-Json | Out-File audit.json

PowerShell features: variables start with $, objects have properties (.Name), Where-Object/Select-Object/Sort-Object, functions with param(), Export-Csv and ConvertTo-Json for reports, Try/Catch for errors.
lessons.analogy: Bash passes notes (text) between workers; PowerShell passes labelled parcels (objects) so the next worker knows exactly what is inside.
lessons.example: A Windows admin used a PowerShell script to check 300 machines for disabled firewalls and produced a CSV for the security team in minutes.
lessons.relevance: Audit scripts make checks repeatable and provide evidence; attackers also use these shells, so defenders monitor them.
practice: Write a Bash script that counts files in a directory passed as $1
Write a PowerShell command that lists stopped services
Export a PowerShell result to CSV
lessons.challenge: Extend quick-audit.sh to write its output to a timestamped file.
mistakes: Unquoted variables in Bash
Treating PowerShell output as plain text instead of objects
Running audit scripts on systems you do not own
lessons.summary: Bash chains text-based tools; PowerShell pipes objects. Both turn manual checks into repeatable, evidenced audits.
lessons.examTip: Remember $? holds the last exit code in Bash, and 0 means success.

quiz.q: In Bash, what does $1 contain?
What does PowerShell pass through a pipeline?
What does an exit code of 0 mean in Bash?

lessons.title: JavaScript, the DOM and Browser Security
lessons.why: Web application testing is impossible without reading JavaScript; client-side flaws like XSS live here.
objectives: Read basic JavaScript
Explain the DOM and web requests
Describe the same-origin policy and client-side security limits
lessons.simple: JavaScript runs in the browser and makes pages interactive. The DOM (Document Object Model) is the browser's tree of page elements that JavaScript can read and change. fetch() sends web requests from the page. Browsers enforce security rules like the same-origin policy, which stops one website's scripts from reading another site's data. Anything in the browser can be viewed and changed by the user, so security checks must always be repeated on the server.
lessons.detailed:
Basics: let/const variables, functions, arrays, objects, events (button.addEventListener("click", ...)), JSON.

DOM: document.getElementById("msg").textContent = userInput; (safe - treats input as text)
versus .innerHTML = userInput; (dangerous - interprets input as HTML, enabling XSS).

Requests: fetch("/api/profile").then(r => r.json()). Cookies with the HttpOnly flag cannot be read by JavaScript; Secure means HTTPS only; SameSite limits cross-site sending (helps against CSRF).

Browser security model: same-origin policy (scheme + host + port must match); CORS lets servers relax it deliberately - misconfigured CORS (e.g. reflecting any origin with credentials) is a vulnerability; Content Security Policy (CSP) restricts where scripts can load from and reduces XSS impact.

Client-side security concepts: hidden form fields, disabled buttons and JavaScript validation are for user experience only - an attacker can bypass them with developer tools or a proxy. Never store secrets (API keys, admin passwords) in front-end code.

Secure development: use textContent or framework escaping, avoid eval(), set CSP, HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite cookies, validate on the server.
lessons.analogy: Client-side validation is a 'please wipe your feet' sign; server-side validation is the security guard at the door.
lessons.example: A shop calculated prices in JavaScript and trusted the total sent by the browser. Testers changed the price in a proxy and 'bought' items for £0.01 - a business logic flaw.
lessons.relevance: XSS, CSRF, CORS issues and exposed secrets in JavaScript are core web findings.
practice: Open browser developer tools on a site you own and inspect the DOM
Find which cookies a lab site sets and their flags
Rewrite an innerHTML line using textContent
lessons.challenge: Explain why a 'maxlength' attribute on a form field is not a security control.
mistakes: Trusting client-side validation
Using innerHTML with user data
Hiding API keys in minified JavaScript
lessons.summary: JavaScript controls the page via the DOM, but the browser belongs to the user. Validate on the server and use browser protections.
lessons.examTip: Same origin = same scheme, host and port. HttpOnly stops JavaScript reading a cookie.

quiz.q: Which DOM property safely inserts untrusted text?
Which cookie flag prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie?
Client-side JavaScript validation is enough to stop malicious input.
quiz.explain: Users control the browser; validate on the server.

lessons.title: SQL: Queries, Joins, Permissions and SQL Injection Prevention
lessons.why: Databases hold the crown jewels. SQL injection remains one of the most damaging web vulnerabilities.
objectives: Write SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE queries
Join tables and apply database permissions
Explain SQL injection and prevent it with parameterised queries
lessons.simple: A relational database stores data in tables of rows and columns. SQL (Structured Query Language) reads and changes it: SELECT reads, INSERT adds, UPDATE changes and DELETE removes. JOIN combines related tables. Database accounts should have only the permissions they need. SQL injection happens when an application builds a query by pasting user input into SQL text, letting an attacker change the query's meaning. The fix is parameterised queries, which keep data separate from code.
lessons.analogy: A parameterised query is a form with fixed boxes: whatever the user writes stays inside its box and can never rewrite the form itself.
lessons.example: Many large data breaches started with a single injectable parameter in a login or search form, exposing entire customer tables.
lessons.relevance: SQLi is tested in nearly every web assessment, and secure database design is a core AppSec skill.
practice: Write a query listing assets owned by 'finance'
Write a JOIN between users and logins
Rewrite a string-concatenated query as a parameterised one
lessons.challenge: Explain to a developer, in plain language, why escaping quotes manually is weaker than parameterised queries.
mistakes: Building SQL with string concatenation
Using a database admin account for the web app
Showing raw SQL errors to users
lessons.summary: SQL reads and changes tables; joins connect them; least-privilege accounts limit damage; parameterised queries stop SQL injection.
lessons.examTip: The primary fix for SQL injection is always parameterised queries (prepared statements).

quiz.q: Which statement reads data?
What is the primary defence against SQL injection?
quiz.explain: Prepared statements separate code from data.

quiz.q: The input ' OR '1'='1 is dangerous in a concatenated query because...
options: It makes the WHERE condition always true
quiz.explain: It alters query logic so every row matches.

lessons.title: Security Automation: Logs, Validation, Integrity and Reports
lessons.why: Automation lets one analyst do the work of many and makes checks consistent and auditable.
objectives: Parse logs automatically
Validate input safely
Build file-integrity checks and automated reports
lessons.simple: Security automation means writing scripts that do repetitive security checks for you: parsing logs for failed logins, validating input, checking files have not changed, and producing reports. A file integrity check stores a hash (fingerprint) of important files and alerts if a hash changes. Always build defensive scripts that read and report rather than change systems, unless the change is approved.
lessons.analogy: A file integrity check is like photographing your room before leaving and comparing photos when you return.
lessons.example: A web server's integrity monitor flagged a changed index.php at 01:12 - the first sign of a web shell, caught within minutes.
lessons.relevance: Detection engineering and blue team roles rely on automating these exact checks.
practice: Run the integrity script on files in your lab VM and then change one file
Write a validator for port numbers (1-65535)
Create a CSV report of failed logins per IP
lessons.challenge: Design an automated weekly report that lists new local admin accounts across your lab machines.
mistakes: Using MD5 for integrity where tampering is a concern
Cleaning bad input instead of rejecting it
Scripts that change systems without approval
lessons.summary: Automate read-only checks: parse logs, validate input with allow-lists, hash files for integrity and produce dated reports.
lessons.examTip: Allow-listing (accept known good) is preferred over deny-listing (block known bad).

quiz.q: What does a file integrity monitor compare?
Which validation approach is strongest?
Which tool category aggregates and analyses logs at scale?
quiz.explain: A SIEM collects and correlates logs.

title: Cybersecurity Fundamentals
intro: This module gives you the vocabulary and mental models of the profession: the CIA triad, identity, cryptography, risk, controls, incident response and - most importantly - the ethics and law that separate an ethical hacker from a criminal.
objectives: Apply the CIA triad and AAA
Explain encryption, hashing, signatures and PKI
Assess threats, vulnerabilities and risk
Choose controls using defence in depth, zero trust and least privilege
Describe incident response phases
Work within ethics, law, privacy and rules of engagement

lessons.title: CIA Triad, AAA, Identity, MFA and Password Security
lessons.why: Every security decision protects confidentiality, integrity or availability - and almost every breach involves identity.
objectives: Define confidentiality, integrity and availability
Explain authentication, authorisation and accounting
Describe MFA and modern password guidance
lessons.simple: The CIA triad lists what security protects: Confidentiality (only authorised people see data), Integrity (data is accurate and unaltered) and Availability (systems work when needed). AAA describes access control: Authentication proves who you are, Authorisation decides what you may do, and Accounting (auditing) records what you did. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) combines two or more factor types - something you know, have or are - so a stolen password alone is not enough.
lessons.detailed:
Examples: ransomware attacks availability (and often confidentiality via data theft); a tampered bank transfer attacks integrity; a leaked database attacks confidentiality.

Identity management covers the lifecycle: joiner (create account with correct access), mover (adjust access when roles change), leaver (disable promptly). Orphaned accounts of former staff are a frequent finding.

Authentication factors: knowledge (password, PIN), possession (phone app, hardware key), inherence (fingerprint, face). Two passwords = still one factor.

MFA strength (strongest first): FIDO2/passkeys and hardware security keys (phishing-resistant) -> authenticator app with number matching -> app push -> SMS codes (vulnerable to SIM swap) . Watch for MFA fatigue attacks (spamming push requests).

Password guidance (NIST SP 800-63B, NCSC): favour length over complexity (passphrases), check new passwords against breached-password lists, do not force periodic changes without evidence of compromise, allow password managers and paste, rate-limit and lock out guessing. Store passwords only as salted, slow hashes (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2).
lessons.analogy: CIA is a bank vault: only the right people get in (confidentiality), nobody can secretly change the ledger (integrity), and the bank opens on time (availability).
lessons.example: Many account takeovers come from reused passwords stolen in other breaches. Organisations that enforced phishing-resistant MFA saw these attacks fail.
lessons.relevance: Your findings will be described by their impact on CIA, and identity weaknesses are among the most common critical issues.
practice: Classify five incidents by the CIA property they affect
List the MFA methods you use and rank them
Check a password idea in the in-app strength analyser (do not use real passwords)
lessons.challenge: Write a short password policy for a small business that follows NIST/NCSC guidance.
mistakes: Thinking two passwords is MFA
Forcing 90-day password changes by default
Confusing authentication with authorisation
lessons.summary: Protect C, I and A. Authenticate, authorise, account. Prefer phishing-resistant MFA and long passphrases stored as slow salted hashes.
lessons.examTip: If asked which MFA is most phishing-resistant: FIDO2/hardware security keys.

quiz.q: A DDoS attack mainly affects...
Checking whether a logged-in user may delete a record is...
Which MFA method is most resistant to phishing?
quiz.explain: FIDO2 binds authentication to the genuine site.

lessons.title: Cryptography: Encryption, Hashing, Signatures, Certificates and PKI
lessons.why: Cryptography protects data at rest and in transit. Testers routinely find weak or misused crypto.
objectives: Compare symmetric and asymmetric encryption
Explain hashing and why it is not encryption
Describe digital signatures, certificates and PKI
lessons.simple: Encryption scrambles data so only someone with the key can read it. Symmetric encryption uses one shared key (AES) and is fast. Asymmetric encryption uses a key pair: a public key anyone can have and a private key you keep secret (RSA, elliptic curve). Hashing turns data into a fixed-length fingerprint that cannot be reversed (SHA-256); it proves integrity. A digital signature uses your private key to prove you created something. Certificates bind a public key to an identity, and a PKI (public key infrastructure) of trusted certificate authorities vouches for them.
lessons.detailed:
Symmetric: AES-128/256 (use GCM mode for authenticated encryption), ChaCha20-Poly1305. Problem: securely sharing the key.
Asymmetric: RSA (2048+ bits), ECC (P-256, Curve25519). Slower; used to exchange symmetric keys and to sign.
TLS combines both: an asymmetric key exchange (ECDHE) agrees a symmetric session key, then AES/ChaCha20 encrypts the traffic.

Hashing: SHA-256/SHA-3 for integrity. MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for collision resistance - do not use them for security. Password storage needs SLOW salted hashes (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2), not fast SHA-256.
Encoding (Base64) vs encryption (needs a key) vs hashing (one-way).

Digital signature: hash the message, sign the hash with the private key; anyone verifies with the public key. Provides integrity, authentication and non-repudiation.

Certificates (X.509): subject, issuer, validity dates, public key, signature of the CA. Chain of trust: root CA -> intermediate CA -> server certificate. Browsers trust roots in their trust store. Revocation via CRL/OCSP. Common findings: expired certificates, self-signed certificates on public services, weak protocols (SSLv3, TLS 1.0/1.1), weak ciphers.

Future: post-quantum algorithms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA standardised by NIST in 2024) are being rolled out to replace RSA/ECC for long-term security.
lessons.analogy: Symmetric crypto is one key for a padlock both people copy; asymmetric is a post box: anyone can drop a letter in (public key), only you can open it (private key).
lessons.example: A tester found an internal portal still accepting TLS 1.0 with weak ciphers and a certificate that expired 14 months earlier - two findings in one service.
lessons.relevance: You will assess TLS configurations, password storage, signatures and certificate hygiene.

mistakes: Calling hashing 'encryption'

lessons.summary: Symmetric for speed, asymmetric for key exchange and signatures, hashing for integrity, slow salted hashes for passwords, PKI for trust.

lessons.title: Threats, Vulnerabilities, Exploits, Risk and Attack Surface
lessons.why: Clear terminology makes your reports credible and your risk ratings defensible.
objectives: Distinguish threat, vulnerability, exploit and risk
Calculate risk from likelihood and impact
Map an attack surface
lessons.simple: A vulnerability is a weakness (an unpatched server). A threat is something that could exploit it (a criminal group). An exploit is the method or code that takes advantage of the weakness. Risk is the chance and consequence of harm: commonly risk = likelihood x impact. The attack surface is everything an attacker could interact with: open ports, web forms, APIs, email, staff and suppliers.
lessons.detailed:
Threat actors: cybercriminals (financial), nation-state groups (espionage), hacktivists (ideology), insiders (malicious or careless), script kiddies. Threat vectors: phishing, exposed services, stolen credentials, supply chain, removable media, misconfiguration.

Risk calculation example (1-5 scales): internet-facing VPN with a critical known vulnerability: likelihood 5, impact 5 = 25 (critical). Internal printer with default password: likelihood 3, impact 2 = 6 (low-medium).

Risk treatment: mitigate (apply controls), transfer (insurance, contracts), avoid (stop the activity), accept (documented, by an accountable owner).

Attack surface categories: digital (servers, apps, APIs, cloud), physical (offices, devices), human (staff, social engineering), third-party (vendors, libraries). Reducing attack surface - removing unused services, accounts and exposure - is one of the most effective controls.

Frameworks: MITRE ATT&CK catalogues real adversary tactics and techniques; the Cyber Kill Chain describes attack stages.
lessons.analogy: A vulnerability is an unlocked window; the threat is a burglar in the area; the exploit is climbing through the window; risk is how likely and how bad a burglary would be.
lessons.example: Two organisations with the same vulnerability had different risk: one exposed it to the internet, the other only to an isolated lab.
lessons.relevance: Reports rate findings by risk, not just by how clever the technique was.
practice: Classify five statements as threat, vulnerability, exploit or risk
Rate three scenarios with a 5x5 matrix
List your home's digital attack surface
lessons.challenge: Build a risk register with five risks for a small online shop (see Practice Centre template).
mistakes: Using 'threat' and 'vulnerability' interchangeably
Rating severity without considering exposure
Accepting risk without an owner
lessons.summary: Weakness + threat + exploit = risk. Rate by likelihood and impact, treat by mitigate/transfer/avoid/accept, and shrink the attack surface.
lessons.examTip: Know the four risk treatments and who may accept risk (an accountable owner).

lessons.title: Security Controls, Defence in Depth, Zero Trust, Policies and Governance
lessons.why: Recommendations in your reports are controls. Knowing control types lets you recommend fixes that actually fit.
objectives: Classify controls by type and function
Apply defence in depth, zero trust and least privilege
Explain policies, standards and governance
lessons.simple: Security controls reduce risk. They can be technical (firewalls, MFA), administrative (policies, training) or physical (locks, badges), and they can prevent, detect or correct problems. Defence in depth layers several controls so one failure does not cause a breach. Zero trust means never trusting a request just because it comes from inside the network - always verify identity, device and context. Least privilege means giving only the access needed. Policies and governance set the rules and accountability that keep this consistent.
lessons.detailed:
Control functions: preventive (MFA, firewall), detective (IDS, logs, CCTV), corrective (backups restore, patching), deterrent (warning banners), compensating (extra monitoring when a fix is impossible).

Defence in depth example for email: SPF/DKIM/DMARC -> email filtering -> link sandboxing -> user training -> endpoint protection -> MFA -> least privilege -> monitoring -> backups.

Zero trust principles (NIST SP 800-207): verify explicitly, least-privilege access, assume breach; enforce per-request decisions using identity, device health and context; micro-segment.

Secure configuration: baselines such as CIS Benchmarks; remove defaults; configuration management to prevent drift.

Policy hierarchy: policy (high-level intent, e.g. 'all access requires MFA') -> standards (mandatory specifics) -> procedures (step-by-step) -> guidelines (recommended).

Governance: roles and accountability (board, CISO, asset owners), frameworks (NIST CSF 2.0 functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover; ISO/IEC 27001), metrics and audits.
lessons.analogy: Defence in depth is a castle: moat, wall, gate, guards and a keep - attackers must beat all of them.
lessons.example: An organisation without MFA but with good logging detected a credential-stuffing attack (detective control) and then deployed MFA (preventive) - showing why both types matter.
lessons.relevance: Your remediation advice must name practical controls, and many audits map findings to NIST CSF or ISO 27001.
practice: Classify ten controls as preventive, detective or corrective
Design a five-layer defence for a laptop
Write a one-line policy and a matching standard
lessons.challenge: Write an access-control policy for a fictional clinic using least privilege and MFA (Practice Centre task).
mistakes: Relying on a single control
Trusting all internal traffic
Writing policies nobody can follow
lessons.summary: Layer preventive, detective and corrective controls; verify everything (zero trust); grant minimal access; govern with policies and frameworks.
lessons.examTip: NIST CSF 2.0 added 'Govern' as a sixth function - expect it in modern exams.

quiz.q: A backup restore is which type of control?

lessons.title: Incident Response, Awareness, Ethics, Law, Privacy and Rules of Engagement
lessons.why: Ethics and authorisation are what make hacking legal. This lesson is the most important in the course.
objectives: Describe the incident response lifecycle
Explain the legal and ethical boundaries of security testing
Define rules of engagement and scope
lessons.simple: Incident response is the organised way to handle security incidents: prepare, detect and analyse, contain, eradicate, recover and learn lessons. Security awareness trains people to spot phishing and report problems. Ethical hacking is only legal with explicit, written authorisation from the system owner. Laws such as the UK Computer Misuse Act 1990 and the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act make unauthorised access a crime, even if you 'meant well'. Privacy laws like UK/EU GDPR govern how personal data is handled - including any you see during testing.
lessons.detailed:
Incident response (NIST SP 800-61): Preparation -> Detection & Analysis -> Containment, Eradication & Recovery -> Post-Incident Activity (lessons learned). Preserve evidence and keep a timeline.

Legal essentials (informational, not legal advice):
• UK Computer Misuse Act 1990: unauthorised access, access with intent to commit further offences, unauthorised acts impairing operation, and making/supplying tools for these offences.
• US CFAA; EU directive on attacks against information systems; Nigeria Cybercrimes Act 2015; Ghana Cybersecurity Act 2020; similar laws worldwide.
• GDPR: lawful basis, data minimisation, security of processing, breach notification (72 hours to the regulator where required).

Rules of engagement (RoE) define: scope (in-scope IPs, domains, apps), out-of-scope systems, testing windows, permitted techniques (e.g. no denial of service, no social engineering unless agreed), data handling, emergency contacts and stop conditions. Authorisation must come from someone who actually has authority over the systems - not just any employee. Cloud and third-party hosted systems may need the provider's rules too.

Professional ethics (e.g. (ISC)2 and EC-Council codes): act honourably and legally, protect confidentiality, avoid harm, report honestly, disclose responsibly.
lessons.analogy: Testing without authorisation is like a locksmith breaking into houses 'to show they are insecure' - it is still burglary.
lessons.example: Security researchers have faced prosecution for accessing systems beyond what they were permitted, even with good intentions. Clear written scope protects everyone.
lessons.relevance: No authorisation, no test. Every lab and project in this app enforces scope, and your capstone is scored on scope compliance.
practice: List the six items every rules-of-engagement document should contain
Read the Lab Rules in the Labs centre
Identify one cybercrime law in your country
lessons.challenge: A friend asks you to 'check' their employer's website for vulnerabilities. Write your reply explaining what authorisation would be needed.
mistakes: Testing 'just a little' outside scope
Accepting verbal permission
Keeping client data after an engagement
lessons.summary: Respond to incidents in phases, train people, and test only with written authorisation, clear scope and respect for privacy law.
lessons.examTip: Any exam scenario without written authorisation has one correct answer: do not test.

title: Reconnaissance & Information Gathering
intro: Reconnaissance is about understanding a target organisation's exposure before testing it. Done ethically it stays inside scope, respects privacy and separates facts from assumptions. All practice here uses fictional organisations and supplied datasets.
objectives: Distinguish passive and active reconnaissance
Analyse DNS, WHOIS and subdomain data
Identify technologies and metadata exposure
Use OSINT tools responsibly
Document reconnaissance with confirmed facts and clear assumptions

lessons.title: Reconnaissance Overview: Passive, Active, OSINT and Scope
lessons.why: Good recon finds the forgotten server; bad recon breaks the law or invades privacy.
objectives: Define passive and active reconnaissance
Explain OSINT and its ethical limits
Validate scope before collecting data
lessons.simple: Reconnaissance is gathering information about a target. Passive recon uses public sources without touching the target's systems (search engines, public DNS, certificate logs). Active recon interacts with the target directly (resolving its DNS servers, visiting its website, scanning) and must be authorised. OSINT (open-source intelligence) is intelligence built from publicly available information. 'Public' does not mean 'anything goes': collect only what the engagement needs.
lessons.detailed:
Recon goals: identify in-scope assets (domains, IP ranges, cloud services, apps), technologies, exposed services, email formats and potential social engineering exposure - only if social engineering is in scope.

Scope validation: confirm every discovered asset is owned by the client and listed (or approved) in scope before active testing. A subdomain that resolves to a third-party SaaS provider is usually NOT the client's to test.

Privacy and overcollection: avoid personal social media profiling, family details, home addresses or anything unrelated to the organisation's security posture. Apply data minimisation (GDPR) and store recon data securely; delete it at the end of the engagement per the contract.

Passive sources: search engines, company website, job adverts (reveal technologies), certificate transparency logs (crt.sh), public DNS, WHOIS/RDAP, code repositories, archived pages.
Active techniques (authorised only): DNS queries to the target's name servers, zone transfer attempts, web crawling, port scanning.
lessons.analogy: Passive recon is reading the estate agent's listing and street map; active recon is walking up and trying the door handles - which needs the owner's permission.
lessons.example: Job adverts asking for 'experience with Citrix NetScaler and SAP' told testers which external technologies to look for - without touching any system.
lessons.relevance: Recon shapes the whole engagement. Out-of-scope or privacy-invasive collection can end an engagement and a career.
practice: Read the fictional 'Northwind Health' scope and list what is in and out of scope
Classify ten techniques as passive or active
Write three privacy rules for your recon notes
lessons.challenge: A subdomain shop.client.example points to a third-party e-commerce platform. Is it in scope? What do you do?
mistakes: Treating 'publicly available' as 'permitted'
Collecting staff personal lives
Assuming every discovered subdomain belongs to the client
lessons.summary: Passive first, active only with authorisation, always validate ownership and collect the minimum.
lessons.examTip: Visiting the target's website is often classed as active (it touches their server) - read the question carefully.

quiz.q: Which is passive reconnaissance?
options: Attempting a DNS zone transfer on their server
quiz.explain: CT logs are third-party public records.

quiz.q: A discovered subdomain is hosted by a SaaS vendor. You should...
options: Confirm with the client and vendor rules before any testing
quiz.explain: Ownership and permission must be validated.

quiz.q: Data minimisation applies to reconnaissance notes.
quiz.explain: Collect only what is needed and protect it.

lessons.title: Domains, DNS Records, WHOIS, Subdomains and Internet Exposure
lessons.why: DNS is the map of an organisation's internet presence. Forgotten subdomains are a classic entry point.
objectives: Interpret DNS records for recon
Read WHOIS/RDAP data
Find subdomains and assess internet exposure
lessons.simple: A domain like northwind.example is managed in DNS. Its records reveal mail servers (MX), name servers (NS), web hosts (A/AAAA), aliases (CNAME) and security settings (TXT records with SPF and DMARC). WHOIS or the newer RDAP shows registration details, though personal data is usually redacted. Subdomains (vpn.northwind.example, dev.northwind.example) often reveal services; dev and test hosts are frequently less protected.
lessons.detailed:
Interpreting records:
• MX -> mail provider (e.g. Microsoft 365 or Google), which shapes phishing defences.
• TXT v=spf1 ... -> authorised mail senders; '-all' strict, '~all' soft fail; no SPF or DMARC p=none means spoofing may be easier.
• CNAME pointing to a deleted cloud resource -> possible subdomain takeover risk.
• NS -> who hosts DNS; zone transfers (AXFR) should be refused to the public.

Subdomain discovery (passive): certificate transparency logs, search engines, passive DNS datasets, Amass passive mode. Active: brute-forcing names against the target's DNS - authorised only.

Internet exposure assessment: map each discovered host to IP, owner (cloud/on-prem/third party), purpose and exposure (login page, VPN, remote desktop, admin panel). Shodan and Censys index exposed services from their own scans - viewing their records is passive for you, but treat findings as leads to validate within scope.

Output: an asset inventory table with columns: asset, IP, source, owner verified (Y/N), exposure, notes.
lessons.analogy: DNS records are the building directory in the lobby: they tell you which floor holds mail, which holds the website and where the side entrances are.
lessons.example: A company deleted a cloud app but left dev.company.example as a CNAME to it. Anyone who claimed that cloud name could host content on the company's subdomain - a subdomain takeover.
lessons.relevance: Exposure mapping drives which services you test and which risks you report (weak email security, forgotten dev hosts).
practice: Open the Recon lab dataset for Silverline and list MX, SPF and DMARC findings
Identify any CNAME that points to an unclaimed resource
Build an asset inventory table
lessons.challenge: From a supplied list of 12 subdomains, choose the three most interesting for testing and justify each.
mistakes: Running active brute-force without permission
Ignoring email security records
Reporting unverified assets as facts
lessons.summary: Read MX, NS, TXT and CNAME records; discover subdomains passively first; verify ownership; inventory exposure.
lessons.examTip: DMARC p=none means 'monitor only' - it does not block spoofed mail.

quiz.q: Which DNS record reveals a domain's mail servers?

DMARC policy p=none means...

lessons.title: Metadata, Technology Identification, Search Engines and Social Engineering Awareness
lessons.why: Documents, headers and search results leak usernames, software versions and internal paths.
objectives: Analyse document metadata
Identify web technologies
Use search operators responsibly and recognise social engineering risk
lessons.simple: Metadata is data about data. Office documents and PDFs can contain author names, usernames, software versions and internal file paths. Photos can contain GPS coordinates. Web servers reveal technologies through headers (Server: nginx), cookies (PHPSESSID suggests PHP) and page source. Search engine operators like site: and filetype: narrow results. Social engineering manipulates people; understanding what an organisation exposes about its staff helps defend against it.
lessons.detailed:
Metadata examples (from a fictional supplied PDF): Author: j.smith; Creator: Microsoft Word 2016; Producer: macOS Quartz; Path: \\fs01\finance\Q3. Insights: username format (first initial.surname), an internal file server name, older Office version. Tools: exiftool (read metadata of files you are authorised to analyse).

Technology identification: HTTP response headers, favicon hashes, error pages, JavaScript libraries, Wappalyzer-style fingerprints, TLS certificate details.

Search operators: site:northwind.example filetype:pdf; inurl:login site:northwind.example; intitle:"index of". Use them only to find information about in-scope organisations and stop if you encounter sensitive personal data - report exposure, do not collect it.

Social engineering awareness: phishing, vishing (phone), smishing (SMS), pretexting, tailgating. Exposure factors: staff lists, email formats, org charts, help-desk processes. Defences: training, verification procedures, reporting channels, MFA, least privilege.
lessons.analogy: Metadata is the fingerprints left on a letter - the letter's words are harmless, but the prints show who handled it.
lessons.example: A council's published PDFs revealed 40 usernames and the internal server name; the remediation was metadata scrubbing before publication.
lessons.relevance: Metadata exposure, verbose headers and outdated technologies are common low-to-medium findings; they also feed later testing.
practice: Analyse the sample metadata in the Recon lab
Identify three technologies from the sample HTTP headers
Write two search operators for in-scope PDFs
lessons.challenge: Write a short recommendation to stop metadata leaks in published documents.
mistakes: Collecting personal data you stumble on
Assuming headers are always accurate (they can be faked)
Running social engineering without explicit scope
lessons.summary: Metadata, headers and search results leak useful facts. Use them in scope, minimise personal data and recommend scrubbing and awareness.
lessons.examTip: Expect questions on which operator restricts results to a domain (site:) or file type (filetype:).

lessons.title: Recon Tools and Documentation: Maltego, theHarvester, Amass and Reporting
lessons.why: Tools speed up recon; documentation turns raw data into evidence you can defend.
objectives: Describe what Maltego, theHarvester and Amass do
Use WHOIS and DNS utilities
Write a recon report that separates facts from assumptions
lessons.simple: Maltego visualises relationships between domains, IPs, people and organisations as graphs. theHarvester collects emails, names, subdomains and hosts from public sources. OWASP Amass performs in-depth subdomain enumeration and attack surface mapping. Simple utilities like whois, dig and nslookup query registration and DNS data. Whatever tools you use, your recon report must state sources, timestamps and confidence, and clearly separate confirmed facts from assumptions.
lessons.detailed:
Tool overview (use against in-scope or fictional targets only):
• whois / RDAP: registrar, dates, name servers.
• dig northwind.example MX +short; dig -x 203.0.113.10 (reverse); nslookup.
• theHarvester -d northwind.example -b <public source> - gathers emails/hosts from search engines and public APIs (some sources need free API keys).
• Amass enum -passive -d northwind.example - passive subdomain enumeration.
• Maltego Community Edition (free with registration) - graph-based link analysis using 'transforms'.

Documentation template:
Finding: dev.northwind.example resolves to 198.51.100.24
Source: crt.sh certificate log, 2026-03-02 10:14 UTC
Status: CONFIRMED (resolves) / Ownership: UNVERIFIED - awaiting client confirmation
Assumption: likely a development server (based on name only)

Confidence levels: confirmed (directly verified), probable (multiple sources), possible (single unverified source). Never state an assumption as a fact in a report.

Preventing overcollection: define collection goals before starting, set time limits, exclude personal social media, store data encrypted, delete on schedule.
lessons.analogy: Recon notes are like a detective's case file: each clue records where it came from, when, and how sure you are.
lessons.example: A report claimed a server ran an outdated CMS based only on a banner; the banner was stale. Marking it 'possible' would have avoided a false finding.
lessons.relevance: Clear, sourced recon is what makes later findings credible in front of clients and auditors.

Mark each as confirmed, probable or possible
lessons.challenge: Convert a messy list of 25 recon results into a clean asset inventory with confidence ratings.
mistakes: Pasting raw tool output into reports
Missing timestamps and sources
Stating guesses as facts
lessons.summary: Tools gather; analysts verify. Every recon item needs a source, time, status and confidence.
lessons.examTip: Know which tool is graph-based (Maltego) and which focuses on subdomain enumeration (Amass).

title: Scanning & Enumeration
intro: Scanning turns an asset list into a map of hosts, ports and services. You will learn how scans work, how to read results, why they are sometimes wrong and how to scan safely inside an authorised lab.
objectives: Discover hosts and map networks
Explain TCP/UDP port states and scan types
Enumerate services and fingerprint operating systems
Interpret Nmap output and recognise false positives
Follow a safe scanning methodology

lessons.title: Network Discovery, Host Discovery and Network Mapping
lessons.why: You cannot assess what you have not found - but finding hosts must stay within scope.
objectives: Explain host discovery techniques
Map live hosts to a network diagram
Respect scope during discovery
lessons.simple: Host discovery finds which IP addresses in a range have live devices. Tools send probes - ICMP echo (ping), TCP packets to common ports, or ARP requests on local networks - and see which addresses answer. Nmap's ping scan (nmap -sn 10.10.10.0/24) lists live hosts without scanning their ports. The results become a network map showing hosts, subnets and gateways.
lessons.detailed:
Discovery methods:
• ARP scan (local subnet only) - very reliable because devices must answer ARP.
• ICMP echo/timestamp - often blocked by firewalls.
• TCP SYN to 443 / TCP ACK to 80 - finds hosts that block ping.
• Reverse DNS - names can reveal roles (dc01, sql-prod).

Nmap: nmap -sn <range> (discovery only); -Pn skips discovery and treats every host as up (useful when ICMP is blocked, but slower); --exclude <ip> to protect out-of-scope hosts; -iL targets.txt to read an approved target list.

Network mapping: group hosts by subnet and role (servers, workstations, network devices, printers, IoT); note gateways and unexpected devices (a personal router plugged into the LAN).

Scope safety: always scan from an approved target file; double-check CIDR; exclude fragile systems listed in the RoE (e.g. medical devices, legacy OT).
lessons.analogy: Host discovery is knocking on every door on a street to see which houses are occupied, before deciding which to inspect.
lessons.example: During an internal test, discovery revealed a forgotten Windows Server 2008 machine nobody had on the asset list - itself a significant finding.
lessons.relevance: Accurate discovery creates the target list for every later phase and reveals unmanaged assets.
practice: Run the Scanning Simulator lab and discover hosts in 10.10.10.0/24
Draw the network map from the results
Identify which host might be a domain controller
lessons.challenge: Explain why '-Pn' can be necessary and why it makes scans slower.
mistakes: Scanning a typed range instead of the approved file
Assuming no ping reply = no host
Ignoring exclusions in the rules of engagement
lessons.summary: Find live hosts with suitable probes, map them by role and never stray outside the approved targets.
lessons.examTip: Remember ARP discovery only works on the local subnet.

lessons.title: Ports, Port States, TCP/UDP Scanning and Firewall Behaviour
lessons.why: Reading port states correctly is the difference between a real finding and a false alarm.
objectives: Explain open, closed and filtered states
Compare SYN, connect and UDP scans
Recognise how firewalls change results
lessons.simple: A port is open when a service is listening and accepts connections, closed when the host answers but nothing is listening, and filtered when no answer comes back because a firewall drops the probe. A TCP SYN scan sends the first handshake packet and watches the reply: SYN-ACK means open, RST means closed, nothing means filtered. UDP scanning is slower and less certain because many UDP services do not reply.
lessons.detailed:
Nmap scan types:
• -sS SYN ('half-open') scan - default when run with privileges; does not complete the handshake.
• -sT connect scan - completes the handshake; used without raw-socket privileges; more likely to be logged.
• -sU UDP scan - open|filtered ambiguity is common; slow because of retransmissions.
• -p 22,80,443 specific ports; -p- all 65,535 TCP ports; --top-ports 1000 (default is the top 1,000).

States: open, closed, filtered, unfiltered (ACK scan), open|filtered, closed|filtered.

Firewall behaviour: stateful firewalls drop (filtered) or reject (closed-looking RST/ICMP unreachable). Rate limiting and IPS can block your scanner part-way through - results may then show everything filtered. Timing: -T3 default; -T4 faster on reliable networks; avoid aggressive timing on fragile networks.

Scan limitations: a closed or filtered port today may open tomorrow; results describe one moment from one network position; scanning from inside vs outside gives very different views.
lessons.analogy: Open = someone answers the door; closed = someone shouts 'nobody here'; filtered = a guard at the gate silently ignores you.
lessons.example: An external scan showed 3389 filtered; the same scan from the guest Wi-Fi showed it open - revealing a segmentation gap.
lessons.relevance: Port states drive findings like 'RDP exposed to the internet' and help verify firewall rules.
practice: In the simulator, run a SYN scan and classify each port state
Explain one open|filtered UDP result
Compare internal vs external scan results
lessons.challenge: A full TCP scan shows every port filtered after port 2,000. What might have happened and how would you confirm it?
mistakes: Treating filtered as closed
Assuming the default 1,000 ports are 'all ports'
Using aggressive timing on fragile networks
lessons.summary: Open accepts, closed rejects, filtered is silent. Scan type, firewall and position all shape what you see.
lessons.examTip: Know which reply maps to which state in a SYN scan.

quiz.q: In a SYN scan, a SYN-ACK reply means the port is...
No response to a SYN probe usually means...

lessons.title: Service Enumeration, OS Fingerprinting and Nmap in Practice
lessons.why: Knowing that port 445 is open is not enough - you need the service, version and configuration.
objectives: Enumerate service versions
Explain OS fingerprinting concepts
Read Nmap output confidently
lessons.simple: Service enumeration identifies what software runs on each open port and which version. Nmap's -sV sends probes and matches responses against a database. OS fingerprinting (-O) guesses the operating system from subtle differences in how network stacks respond. The Nmap Scripting Engine (NSE) runs scripts for deeper, safe enumeration such as reading SMB security settings or listing supported TLS ciphers.
lessons.detailed:
Example (simulated lab output):
PORT     STATE SERVICE  VERSION
22/tcp   open  ssh      OpenSSH 8.2p1 Ubuntu 4ubuntu0.5
80/tcp   open  http     Apache httpd 2.4.41 ((Ubuntu))
445/tcp  open  microsoft-ds  Samba smbd 4.x
3306/tcp open  mysql    MySQL 5.7.33
Service Info: OS: Linux

Reading it: OpenSSH 8.2p1 + Apache 2.4.41 suggests Ubuntu 20.04; MySQL exposed on the network is a finding to review (should it listen only on localhost?); Samba needs SMB signing and share checks.

Useful options: -sV (versions), -sC (default safe scripts), -O (OS guess), -A (aggressive: -sV -sC -O --traceroute), -oA name (save all formats - always save evidence), --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443, --script smb2-security-mode.

Enumeration by service: HTTP -> headers, titles, robots.txt; SMB -> shares, signing; SNMP -> community strings (public/private defaults); FTP -> anonymous login; DNS -> zone transfer; SMTP -> open relay checks.

OS fingerprinting is a probability, not proof - confirm through other evidence.
lessons.analogy: Port scanning finds the doors; enumeration reads the brand and model of each lock.
lessons.example: Version enumeration showed an internal web server running a CMS version with a publicly known critical vulnerability - which became the top-priority finding.
lessons.relevance: Versions map to CVEs in Module 8; configuration details become findings on their own.
practice: Run -sV and -sC against the lab web server in the simulator
Identify which services should not be network-exposed
Save results conceptually with -oA
lessons.challenge: From the sample output above, list three follow-up checks and why.
mistakes: Trusting version banners blindly
Not saving scan output as evidence
Running intrusive scripts without approval
lessons.summary: Enumerate services and versions, use safe scripts, treat OS guesses as hypotheses and always save output.
lessons.examTip: -A combines -sV, -sC, -O and traceroute.

quiz.q: Which Nmap flag detects service versions?
What does -oA do?
options: Saves output in all major formats

quiz.q: OS fingerprinting results are always certain.
quiz.explain: They are best guesses based on stack behaviour.

lessons.title: Interpreting Results, False Positives, Scanner Limitations and Safe Methodology
lessons.why: Clients pay for accurate findings. Unvalidated scanner output erodes trust and wastes remediation effort.
objectives: Validate scan results
Explain vulnerability scanner limitations
Apply a safe scanning methodology with Nmap, Netcat, Wireshark, OpenVAS and Nessus
lessons.simple: Scanners are fast but imperfect. A false positive is a reported issue that does not exist; a false negative is a real issue the scanner missed. Results must be validated: confirm the service manually, check versions from more than one source and consider whether a backported patch has fixed a flaw even though the version number looks old. Vulnerability scanners such as OpenVAS (free, open source) and Nessus (commercial, with a limited free Essentials edition) automate checks but still need expert interpretation.
lessons.detailed:
Validation techniques:
• Netcat banner check: nc -nv 10.10.10.15 21 (read the banner yourself).
• Wireshark: confirm what the scanner actually sent and received.
• Check package versions on the host (with access) - Linux distributions backport fixes, so 'Apache 2.4.41' may be patched.
• Credentialed scans give far more accurate results than unauthenticated ones.

Scanner limitations: cannot understand business logic; may crash fragile services; miss issues behind authentication; depend on plugin updates; produce noise.

Safe scanning methodology:
1. Confirm written scope, exclusions and testing window.
2. Notify the client's contact/SOC if agreed.
3. Start with discovery, then light port scans, then service enumeration.
4. Use moderate timing; avoid DoS-prone checks unless approved.
5. Monitor for impact; stop and call the emergency contact if a system degrades.
6. Save all output with timestamps.
7. Validate before reporting.
lessons.analogy: A scanner is a smoke detector: very useful, but sometimes it goes off for burnt toast - someone has to check if there is really a fire.
lessons.example: A scanner flagged 300 'critical' OpenSSL issues on a Red Hat estate; most were false positives because Red Hat had backported fixes. Credentialed validation reduced it to 4 real issues.
lessons.relevance: Accurate validation is a core professional skill and a scoring criterion in your capstone.
practice: Complete the Scanning Simulator lab end-to-end
Validate one 'finding' with a Netcat banner grab in the simulator
Mark a sample scanner result as true or false positive
lessons.challenge: Write the stop conditions you would agree with a hospital client before scanning.
mistakes: Copying scanner output straight into a report
Running intrusive plugins on production without approval
Ignoring backporting
lessons.summary: Validate everything, understand scanner limits and follow a scoped, monitored, documented methodology.
lessons.examTip: A credentialed scan reduces false positives - a frequent exam answer.

quiz.q: A scanner reports a vulnerability that does not actually exist. This is a...
quiz.explain: Reported but not real = false positive.

quiz.q: Why might an 'old' version number not be vulnerable?
options: The vendor backported a security fix
quiz.explain: Distributions backport patches without changing the upstream version.

quiz.q: What improves vulnerability scan accuracy most?
quiz.explain: Credentials let the scanner check installed packages directly.

Identify open, closed and filtered ports

title: Vulnerability Assessment
intro: Finding vulnerabilities is only half the job. This module teaches how to describe, score, prioritise and drive remediation of vulnerabilities across their lifecycle.
objectives: Run a vulnerability management lifecycle
Use CVE, CVSS, NVD, KEV and EPSS
Prioritise using risk and asset criticality
Handle false positives and negatives through validation
Plan remediation, patching and risk acceptance

lessons.title: Vulnerability Management and the Vulnerability Lifecycle
lessons.why: Organisations do not fail because they lack scanners; they fail because findings never get fixed.
objectives: Describe the vulnerability management cycle
Explain discovery sources
Track vulnerabilities to closure
lessons.simple: Vulnerability management is a continuous cycle: discover assets and vulnerabilities, assess and prioritise them, remediate or mitigate, verify the fix and report. Vulnerabilities are discovered by scanners, penetration tests, bug bounty reports, vendor advisories and threat intelligence. Each one moves through a lifecycle from discovery to disclosure, patch availability, deployment and verification.
lessons.detailed:
Cycle: Asset inventory -> Discovery -> Assessment/validation -> Prioritisation -> Remediation/mitigation -> Verification (rescan/retest) -> Reporting & metrics -> repeat.

Vulnerability lifecycle (from the industry view): introduced in code -> discovered (by vendor, researcher or attacker) -> disclosed (coordinated) -> CVE assigned -> patch released -> exploit published -> patch deployed by customers. The gap between disclosure and deployment is where most attacks happen. A zero-day is exploited before a fix exists.

Metrics: mean time to remediate (MTTR) by severity, SLA compliance (e.g. critical within 14 days), percentage of assets scanned, recurring findings, risk accepted count.

Ownership: every finding needs an owner (system/asset owner) and a due date. Ticketing systems (Jira, ServiceNow, or free tools such as GitHub Issues for small teams) track status: Open -> In progress -> Fixed -> Verified -> Closed (or Risk accepted).
lessons.analogy: Vulnerability management is like a hospital ward round: find problems, decide who is most urgent, treat them, then check the treatment worked.
lessons.example: Many major breaches exploited vulnerabilities whose patches had been available for months - the problem was the remediation process, not detection.
lessons.relevance: Assessors who understand the full lifecycle write findings that are easier for clients to act on.
practice: Map the lifecycle stages to a fictional finding
Define SLAs for critical/high/medium/low
Design ticket statuses
lessons.challenge: Explain why verification (rescanning) is a separate step from remediation.
mistakes: No asset inventory - unknown assets are never scanned
Closing tickets without verification
Findings with no owner
lessons.summary: Discover, prioritise, fix, verify, report - continuously, with owners and SLAs.
lessons.examTip: A zero-day has no available patch at the time it is exploited.

quiz.q: What should happen after a vulnerability is remediated?
options: Verify the fix by rescanning or retesting

quiz.q: A vulnerability exploited before a patch exists is a...
MTTR measures...

lessons.title: CVE, CVSS and Vulnerability Databases (NVD, KEV, EPSS)
lessons.why: These identifiers and scores are the common language between scanners, vendors and clients.
objectives: Read a CVE identifier and record
Calculate and interpret CVSS base scores
Use KEV and EPSS to judge real-world exploitation
lessons.simple: A CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) ID such as CVE-2021-44228 uniquely names a public vulnerability. CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) gives a 0-10 severity score from metrics such as attack vector, complexity, privileges required, user interaction and impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability. The NVD (US National Vulnerability Database) enriches CVEs with scores and details. CISA's KEV catalogue lists vulnerabilities known to be exploited in the wild, and EPSS estimates the probability of exploitation.
lessons.detailed:
CVSS v3.1 base metrics: Attack Vector (Network/Adjacent/Local/Physical), Attack Complexity (Low/High), Privileges Required (None/Low/High), User Interaction (None/Required), Scope (Unchanged/Changed), Confidentiality/Integrity/Availability impact (None/Low/High).
Example vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H = 9.8 Critical.

Severity bands: 0.1-3.9 Low, 4.0-6.9 Medium, 7.0-8.9 High, 9.0-10.0 Critical.

CVSS v4.0 (released 2023) adds supplemental metrics and renames some groups; both versions appear in tools today.

Base score = intrinsic severity. Temporal/threat metrics (exploit maturity) and environmental metrics (your asset's importance and controls) adjust it for your context.

Other sources: vendor advisories, Exploit-DB, GitHub Security Advisories, CWE (weakness categories, e.g. CWE-89 SQL injection). Use the in-app CVSS calculator to practise.
lessons.analogy: A CVE number is a passport number for a vulnerability; CVSS is its danger rating; KEV is the 'wanted - actively seen in attacks' list.
lessons.example: Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) scored CVSS 10.0, appeared in KEV and was exploited at massive scale within days of disclosure.
lessons.relevance: Findings cite CVEs and CVSS; prioritisation increasingly uses KEV and EPSS so effort goes to what attackers actually use.
practice: Use the in-app CVSS calculator to score AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N
Explain what each metric in a vector means
Classify scores 3.1, 6.5, 7.2 and 9.1 into bands
lessons.challenge: Two findings: one CVSS 9.8 not in KEV, one CVSS 7.5 listed in KEV and internet-facing. Which do you fix first and why?
mistakes: Treating CVSS as the full risk picture
Ignoring KEV
Confusing CVE (specific flaw) with CWE (weakness type)
lessons.summary: CVE names it, CVSS rates severity, KEV and EPSS show real-world exploitation, environment and asset value complete the picture.
lessons.examTip: Memorise the CVSS severity bands and the meaning of AV:N and PR:N.

quiz.q: A CVSS score of 7.4 is rated...
What does CISA's KEV catalogue list?
options: Vulnerabilities known to be exploited in the wild

quiz.q: In a CVSS vector, AV:N means...

lessons.title: Risk, Likelihood, Impact, Asset Criticality and Prioritisation
lessons.why: Clients have limited time and money. Your job is to tell them what to fix first and why.
objectives: Combine severity with context
Rate asset criticality
Produce a prioritised remediation list
lessons.simple: Severity describes how bad a vulnerability is in general; risk describes how bad it is for this organisation. Risk combines likelihood (exposure, exploit availability, attacker interest) and impact (what the affected asset does and holds). Asset criticality ranks systems by business importance - a payment database matters more than a test printer. Prioritise findings that are severe, exploitable, exposed and on critical assets.
lessons.detailed:
Prioritisation factors:
• Exposure: internet-facing > internal > isolated.
• Exploitability: KEV-listed / public exploit > proof-of-concept > theoretical.
• Asset criticality: crown jewels (customer data, payments, identity systems like AD) > business systems > low-value.
• Compensating controls: WAF, segmentation, MFA may reduce likelihood.
• Data sensitivity and regulatory impact (GDPR, PCI DSS).

Simple model: Priority = CVSS band adjusted up for KEV/internet exposure/critical asset, down for strong compensating controls.

Example prioritised list:
1. VPN appliance CVE in KEV, internet-facing - Critical, fix in 48h.
2. Domain controller missing patch with public exploit - High, 7 days.
3. Internal intranet XSS, low-sensitivity data - Medium, 30 days.
4. TLS 1.0 enabled on internal printer - Low, next cycle.

Communicate impact in business language: 'An attacker on the internet could take over the VPN and access the internal network without credentials.'
lessons.analogy: Triage in an emergency department: the most serious injuries on the most vulnerable patients are treated first, not simply in arrival order.
lessons.example: A team spent weeks fixing hundreds of low findings while one internet-facing critical issue stayed open - and was exploited. Prioritisation would have reversed that order.
lessons.relevance: Prioritised, business-aware recommendations are what separate a professional report from a scanner dump.
practice: Complete the CVSS Prioritisation lab
Rate five assets by criticality
Rewrite one technical impact in business language
lessons.challenge: Prioritise a list of 10 fictional findings and justify the top three in writing.
mistakes: Sorting by CVSS alone
Ignoring compensating controls
Writing impact only in technical jargon
lessons.summary: Priority = severity in context: exposure, exploitability, asset criticality and controls. Explain it in business terms.
lessons.examTip: Expect scenario questions where the lower CVSS score should be fixed first because of exposure or KEV status.

quiz.q: Which finding should usually be fixed first?
options: CVSS 9.0 on an isolated lab VM
CVSS 8.1 KEV-listed on an internet-facing VPN
quiz.explain: Exposure plus active exploitation drives priority.

quiz.q: Asset criticality measures...
quiz.explain: How important the asset is to the business.

quiz.q: A compensating control can lower the likelihood of exploitation.
quiz.explain: e.g. segmentation or WAF can reduce likelihood.

lessons.title: False Positives, False Negatives, Validation and Scanner Limitations
lessons.why: Validation protects your credibility and the client's resources.
objectives: Classify scanner results correctly
Validate findings safely
Explain what scanners cannot find
lessons.simple: Every scanner result must be treated as a hypothesis. A true positive is a real issue correctly found. A false positive is reported but not real. A false negative is a real issue that was missed - often more dangerous because nobody knows it exists. Validation means confirming a finding with additional evidence, using safe, non-destructive methods within scope.
lessons.detailed:
Causes of false positives: version-only detection with backported patches, generic signatures, unusual services on standard ports, outdated plugins.
Causes of false negatives: unauthenticated scans, services behind login, WAF/IPS blocking probes, non-standard ports not scanned, business logic flaws, timing issues, scope gaps.

Safe validation methods: check installed package versions with credentials; confirm configuration directly (e.g. read sshd_config); manual banner checks; vendor-provided detection scripts; safe proof that demonstrates existence without causing impact (e.g. reading a harmless version endpoint, not dumping data).

Documenting validation: record what you did, when, the evidence (screenshot or output), and why you concluded true/false positive.

Scanner limitations summary: no business context, limited auth coverage, cannot chain issues, cannot judge impact, can disrupt fragile systems.
lessons.analogy: A metal detector beeps (scanner alert). Digging carefully (validation) tells you whether it is treasure, a bottle cap or nothing at all.
lessons.example: A validated false positive saved a hospital from an emergency weekend patch of 200 servers.
lessons.relevance: Your findings list must contain validated issues only - and your report should state the limits of what was tested.
practice: Classify ten sample scanner results as TP/FP with reasons
List four causes of false negatives
Write a validation note
lessons.challenge: Design a validation plan for a 'critical' OpenSSH finding on an Ubuntu server.
mistakes: Exploiting to 'prove' a finding without approval
Assuming no findings means secure
Not documenting validation steps
lessons.summary: Treat results as hypotheses, validate safely, document reasoning and state limitations.
lessons.examTip: False negatives are usually considered more dangerous than false positives.

quiz.q: A real vulnerability that a scanner did not report is a...
Which is a common cause of false negatives?
options: Unauthenticated scanning of services behind login
quiz.explain: The scanner cannot see behind authentication.

quiz.q: Safe validation should...
options: Dump the database to prove impact

lessons.title: Misconfiguration, Patch Management, Remediation and Risk Acceptance
lessons.why: Most real-world weaknesses are misconfigurations and missing patches. Good remediation advice is specific, achievable and verifiable.
objectives: Recognise common misconfigurations
Describe a patch management process
Write remediation plans and handle risk acceptance
lessons.simple: Misconfigurations are insecure settings: default passwords, unnecessary services, open shares, overly permissive cloud storage, weak TLS. Patch management keeps software updated through a controlled process: inventory, test, deploy, verify. Remediation fixes the root cause; mitigation reduces risk when a fix is not yet possible. When an organisation decides not to fix something, an accountable owner must formally accept the risk with a review date.
lessons.detailed:
Common misconfigurations: default credentials; directory listing; verbose errors; SMBv1; anonymous FTP; SNMP 'public'; open S3/Blob storage; admin interfaces exposed to the internet; missing security headers; excessive permissions.

Patch management process: maintain inventory -> monitor advisories -> assess applicability and priority -> test in staging -> schedule (maintenance windows) -> deploy -> verify (rescan) -> report. Emergency patching path for KEV/critical issues.

Remediation plan entries: finding, owner, action (specific: 'Disable TLS 1.0/1.1 in nginx ssl_protocols; allow TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3'), priority, due date, verification method, status.

Mitigation examples when patching is delayed: restrict access with firewall rules, disable the vulnerable feature, add WAF rules, increase monitoring.

Risk acceptance: written, by someone with authority, with reason, compensating controls and an expiry/review date. Not acceptable as a default for critical internet-facing issues.
lessons.analogy: Remediation is fixing the leaking pipe; mitigation is putting a bucket under it until the plumber comes; risk acceptance is the owner signing that they know about the leak.
lessons.example: A company could not patch a legacy system for six months, so it isolated it on a separate VLAN with strict firewall rules and monitoring - a documented mitigation with an expiry date.
lessons.relevance: Your recommendations will be judged on whether they are specific, practical and verifiable.
practice: Write remediation steps for three misconfigurations
Build a mini patch schedule
Draft a risk acceptance record
lessons.challenge: Build a vulnerability remediation plan for the fictional Silverline findings in Project 6.
mistakes: Vague advice like 'improve security'
No verification method
Risk acceptance without an expiry date
lessons.summary: Fix root causes, patch through a tested process, mitigate when you must, and document any accepted risk with an owner and review date.
lessons.examTip: Mitigation reduces risk; remediation removes the vulnerability. Know the difference.

quiz.q: Restricting access to a vulnerable service with a firewall while waiting for a patch is...
quiz.explain: It reduces risk without removing the flaw.

quiz.q: A good risk acceptance includes...
options: An accountable owner and a review date

quiz.q: Which is a misconfiguration?
quiz.explain: Default credentials are a classic misconfiguration.
