title: Web Application Hacking
intro: Web applications are the most exposed part of most organisations. This academy module covers how the web works and the major vulnerability classes, each with what it is, why it happens, how to recognise it, safe lab demonstration, documentation, fixes and verification. All practice uses the built-in simulated 'Silverline Portal' or local deliberately vulnerable apps such as OWASP Juice Shop.
objectives: Explain HTTP, cookies, sessions and web architecture
Test authentication, sessions and access control
Identify and explain injection and XSS flaws
Recognise CSRF, SSRF, file upload, traversal and misconfiguration issues
Assess APIs and business logic
Use Burp Suite, OWASP ZAP and developer tools in a lab

lessons.title: How the Web Works: HTTP, Headers, Cookies, Sessions and Architecture
lessons.why: Every web vulnerability is a misuse of these building blocks.
objectives: Read raw HTTP requests and responses
Explain cookies and session management
Describe front-end/back-end architecture
lessons.simple: A browser sends an HTTP request (method, path, headers, optional body) and the server returns a response (status code, headers, body). HTTPS wraps HTTP in TLS encryption. HTTP is stateless, so sites use cookies holding a session ID to remember who you are after you log in. Modern web apps have a front end (HTML, CSS, JavaScript in the browser), a back end (application server and business logic) and a database, often connected through APIs that exchange JSON.
lessons.detailed:
Raw request:
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: portal.silverline.test
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Cookie: lang=en

username=alice&password=********

Raw response:
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Set-Cookie: SESSIONID=8f3c...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax
Location: /dashboard

Methods: GET (read), POST (create/submit), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE, OPTIONS (CORS preflight). Important headers: Host, Cookie, Authorization, Content-Type, User-Agent, Referer, Origin; response security headers: Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options/frame-ancestors, Referrer-Policy.

Sessions: the session ID must be long, random, sent only over HTTPS, HttpOnly, regenerated after login (prevents fixation) and invalidated on logout/timeout. Tokens such as JWTs carry signed claims - they must be verified server-side and must not use 'alg: none'.

Architecture: browser -> CDN/WAF -> load balancer -> web/app servers -> APIs/microservices -> databases, caches, object storage. Each hop is a trust boundary where input must be validated.
lessons.analogy: HTTP is a series of separate letters; the session cookie is a cloakroom ticket that lets the server remember which coat (account) is yours.
lessons.example: A site that did not set the Secure flag sent session cookies over HTTP on public Wi-Fi, where they could be captured and reused.
lessons.relevance: Burp and ZAP show exactly these requests; reading them fluently is the base skill of web testing.
practice: Open the Web lab and inspect a raw login request
List the security headers missing from the sample response
Explain what each cookie flag does
lessons.challenge: Explain session fixation and how regenerating the session ID after login prevents it.
mistakes: Assuming HTTPS alone makes an app secure
Storing session tokens in localStorage without considering XSS
Forgetting HTTP is stateless
lessons.summary: Requests and responses carry everything; sessions bridge statelessness; every architectural hop is a trust boundary.
lessons.examTip: Know what HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security) does: forces browsers to use HTTPS for the domain.

quiz.q: Which flag stops a cookie being sent over plain HTTP?
Why regenerate the session ID after login?
quiz.explain: An attacker-planted pre-login ID becomes useless.

quiz.q: Which header tells browsers to always use HTTPS for a site?

lessons.title: Authentication, Sessions, Broken Access Control and IDOR
lessons.why: Broken access control is ranked number one in the OWASP Top 10 (2021).
objectives: Assess authentication weaknesses
Identify session weaknesses
Test for broken access control and IDOR in a lab
lessons.simple: Authentication weaknesses let attackers log in as someone else: no rate limiting, default credentials, weak password reset or missing MFA. Session weaknesses let them hijack logged-in users. Broken access control means users can do or see things they should not, such as a normal user opening an admin page. IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) is a common form: changing /invoice?id=1001 to id=1002 shows someone else's invoice because the server never checks ownership.
lessons.detailed:
WHAT IT IS: Access control failures let a user act outside their permissions: horizontal (another user's data) or vertical (admin functions).

WHY IT HAPPENS: Developers rely on hiding links or on the client, or forget to check ownership on every request and API endpoint.

HOW TO RECOGNISE IT: Change object IDs in URLs, bodies and API paths; replay admin requests with a low-privilege session; check whether hidden buttons' endpoints still work.

IMPACT: Data exposure of other customers, privilege escalation to admin, unauthorised changes - often critical.

SAFE DEMONSTRATION (lab only): In the Silverline Portal lab, log in as test user 'learner', request /api/invoices/1001 (yours) then /api/invoices/1002 (belongs to fictional user 'bob') and observe the server returns it.

HOW TO DOCUMENT IT: Title, affected endpoint, roles tested, request/response evidence with personal data redacted, impact in business terms, CVSS.

HOW DEVELOPERS FIX IT: Enforce authorisation server-side on every request using the session identity; deny by default; check object ownership; use indirect references or UUIDs as defence in depth, not as the fix.

HOW TO VERIFY THE FIX: Repeat the same requests with the low-privilege session after the fix; expect 403/404 and no data.

PREVENTION: Centralised authorisation middleware, automated tests per role, logging of access-control failures.

Authentication checks: lockout/rate limiting, MFA availability, password policy, secure reset (single-use, short-lived tokens), username enumeration via different error messages, credentials only over HTTPS.
lessons.analogy: Access control is a hotel key card: the door must check the card against the room every time, not just trust that guests stay on their own floor.
lessons.example: A large telecoms breach involved an API that returned customer records for any sequential ID without checking authorisation.
lessons.relevance: IDOR and privilege escalation are among the most frequent high and critical web findings.
practice: Complete the IDOR task in the Web Security lab
List three places object IDs can appear
Write the fix in one sentence
lessons.challenge: A low-privilege user can call POST /admin/users/delete because the button is only hidden. Write the finding.
mistakes: Testing with real customer accounts instead of test accounts
Assuming random IDs are a fix
Only testing the UI, not the API
lessons.summary: Check authorisation on every request. Test horizontally (other users) and vertically (admin functions) with your own test accounts.
lessons.examTip: Broken Access Control is A01 in the OWASP Top 10 2021.

quiz.q: Changing an order ID in a URL to view another customer's order is...
Where must access control be enforced?
A login page that says 'unknown user' vs 'wrong password' enables...

lessons.title: SQL Injection in Depth
lessons.why: Injection remains in the OWASP Top 10 and can expose entire databases.
objectives: Recognise SQL injection points and behaviour
Explain in-band, blind and error-based SQLi conceptually
Fix and verify with parameterised queries
lessons.simple: SQL injection happens when user input is inserted into a database query as code. Signs include database errors after typing a quote, or results changing when you add logic like AND 1=1 versus AND 1=2. In the lab you will see how a vulnerable login can be bypassed and how the secure version, using parameterised queries, treats the same input as harmless text.
lessons.detailed:
WHAT IT IS: Untrusted input changes the structure of an SQL query.

WHY IT HAPPENS: Queries are built by string concatenation or unsafe ORM raw queries; input is not parameterised.

HOW TO RECOGNISE IT: Error messages after a single quote; differing responses to true/false conditions; time delays; values reflected from UNION queries (lab).

IMPACT: Authentication bypass, reading or modifying any data, sometimes server compromise - typically high or critical.

SAFE DEMONSTRATION (lab only): In the Silverline Portal lab /v1/login, entering a classic tautology as the username shows 'Logged in as admin'. The same input on /v2/login (parameterised) returns 'Invalid credentials'. Types: in-band (error/UNION), blind (boolean/time), out-of-band.

HOW TO DOCUMENT IT: Parameter, endpoint, payload type (described, not a weaponised dump), evidence of behaviour difference, data types exposed (redacted), CVSS, CWE-89.

HOW DEVELOPERS FIX IT: Parameterised queries/prepared statements everywhere; safe ORM methods; least-privilege DB user; generic error pages; input validation as defence in depth.

HOW TO VERIFY THE FIX: Repeat the original test cases on the fixed endpoint; confirm identical behaviour for true/false conditions and no errors.

PREVENTION: Secure coding training, SAST rules for string-built SQL, code review, DAST in CI.

Tools such as sqlmap automate detection and exploitation - only ever use them against lab targets or with explicit authorisation, because they can modify or extract large amounts of data.
lessons.analogy: SQL injection is like a form that says 'Pay ___ pounds' where someone writes '10 to me, and also pay 1,000,000 to me' - and the bank clerk executes it as written.
lessons.example: In real breaches, a single injectable search parameter exposed millions of customer records.
lessons.relevance: SQLi tests appear in every web assessment and in exams such as eJPT, OSCP and BSCP.
practice: Complete the SQL Injection task in the Web Security lab (v1 vs v2)
Explain why the v2 endpoint is safe
Write the remediation for a developer
lessons.challenge: Describe how you would safely demonstrate SQLi impact to a client without extracting real personal data.
mistakes: Running automated SQLi tools against production without approval
Recommending 'escape quotes' instead of parameterisation
Dumping real data as 'proof'
lessons.summary: SQLi = input becomes code. Recognise behaviour changes, demonstrate minimally, fix with parameterised queries and verify.

lessons.title: Cross-Site Scripting (Reflected, Stored, DOM), CSRF and Security Headers
lessons.why: XSS lets attackers run script in victims' browsers; CSRF makes victims perform actions unknowingly.
objectives: Distinguish reflected, stored and DOM XSS
Explain CSRF and its defences
Use output encoding, CSP and headers as mitigations
lessons.simple: Cross-site scripting (XSS) happens when a site includes untrusted input in a page without encoding it, so the browser runs it as script. Reflected XSS comes back immediately from the request (e.g. a search term). Stored XSS is saved (e.g. a comment) and hits every visitor. DOM XSS happens entirely in client-side JavaScript. Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request, like changing their email.
lessons.detailed: WHAT IT IS: XSS: attacker-controlled script executes in another user's browser in the site's origin. CSRF: forged state-changing requests ride on the victim's cookies. WHY IT HAPPENS: XSS: missing context-aware output encoding, innerHTML, unsafe templates. CSRF: state-changing requests rely only on cookies with no anti-CSRF token or SameSite protection. HOW TO RECOGNISE IT: XSS: input reflected unencoded in HTML, attributes or scripts; in the lab a harmless test string like test rendering bold. CSRF: POST forms with no token and cookies without SameSite. IMPACT: Session/account takeover, actions as the victim, defacement, credential prompts; CSRF can change passwords or emails. SAFE DEMONSTRATION (lab only): In the lab comment board (v1), a harmless marker like xss-test renders in italics for every viewer (stored). In v2 it displays as text because output is encoded. For CSRF, the lab shows an email-change form without a token and the fixed version with a token. HOW TO DOCUMENT IT: Context (HTML body, attribute, JS), XSS type, affected page/parameter, harmless proof (e.g. alert of document.domain in lab), impact, CWE-79/CWE-352. HOW DEVELOPERS FIX IT: XSS: context-aware output encoding, framework auto-escaping, textContent, sanitise rich HTML with a vetted library, CSP. CSRF: anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies, re-authentication for sensitive actions, check Origin. HOW TO VERIFY THE FIX: Re-test the same inputs; confirm they render as text and that CSP blocks inline script; confirm forged requests are rejected. PREVENTION: Secure templates, CSP in report-only then enforce, security headers, developer training. Security headers: Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, frame-ancestors / X-Frame-Options (clickjacking), Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, HSTS.
lessons.analogy: XSS is graffiti that turns into instructions for everyone who reads the wall; CSRF is someone forging your signature on a form while you are logged in at the bank.
lessons.example: Stored XSS in a support ticket system let attackers hijack help-desk agents' sessions when they opened tickets.
lessons.relevance: XSS (A03 injection category) and CSRF are core findings and core BSCP/OSCP knowledge.

lessons.title: SSRF, File Uploads, Directory Traversal, Deserialization, Misconfiguration and Information Disclosure
lessons.why: These server-side flaws often lead to internal network access or full server compromise.
objectives: Explain SSRF and its cloud impact
Assess file upload and traversal risks
Recognise deserialization, misconfiguration and disclosure issues
lessons.simple: Server-side request forgery (SSRF) tricks a server into making requests to places the attacker chooses, such as internal services or cloud metadata endpoints. Insecure file uploads let attackers upload dangerous files. Directory (path) traversal uses sequences like ../ to read files outside the intended folder. Insecure deserialization turns attacker-controlled data into objects in dangerous ways. Misconfigurations and information disclosure (stack traces, debug pages, backup files) hand attackers useful details.
lessons.detailed:
SSRF - why: features that fetch URLs (webhooks, image-from-URL, PDF generators) without restricting destinations. Recognise: a parameter containing a URL; in the lab, url=http://127.0.0.1:8080/admin returns internal content. Impact: internal scanning, reaching admin services, cloud credential theft via metadata (AWS IMDSv1). Fix: allow-list destinations, block internal/link-local ranges after DNS resolution, disable redirects, use IMDSv2, network egress controls.

File upload - why: trusting extension/Content-Type, storing uploads in the web root. Recognise: upload features that serve files back from the same domain. Fix: allow-list types, verify content (magic bytes), rename files, store outside the web root or in object storage, set Content-Disposition, scan with antivirus, size limits.

Directory traversal - why: building file paths from input. Recognise: parameters like file=report.pdf; in the lab file=../../etc/hostname returns the simulated host file. Fix: map IDs to files, canonicalise and check the resolved path stays in the base directory.

Insecure deserialization (concept): native object formats (Java serialization, Python pickle, PHP unserialize) on untrusted data can trigger code execution. Fix: use simple data formats like JSON with schema validation, never deserialize untrusted native objects, sign data.

Misconfiguration & disclosure: directory listing, default pages, debug mode, verbose errors, exposed .git or backup files, unnecessary HTTP methods, outdated components (OWASP A05/A06). Fix: hardened baselines, remove samples, generic error pages, automated config checks.

Document each with endpoint, parameter, harmless evidence, impact, CWE (918 SSRF, 434 upload, 22 traversal, 502 deserialization, 200 exposure) and verification steps.
lessons.analogy: SSRF is persuading the company receptionist to phone an internal extension for you; traversal is asking for 'the file in the cupboard behind the cupboard'.
lessons.example: A major cloud breach involved SSRF against a misconfigured WAF that let the attacker reach the instance metadata service and obtain credentials.
lessons.relevance: These flaws commonly chain into the highest-impact findings, especially in cloud-hosted apps.

lessons.title: APIs: REST, JSON, API Vulnerabilities, Rate Limiting and Business Logic
lessons.why: APIs power mobile apps and modern sites; they expose data directly and are frequently under-protected.
objectives: Test REST APIs methodically
Apply the OWASP API Security Top 10
Find rate limiting and business logic flaws
lessons.simple: APIs let programs talk to each other. REST APIs use URLs for resources (/api/v1/users/42) and HTTP methods for actions, usually exchanging JSON. API flaws include broken object-level authorisation (BOLA - the API version of IDOR), excessive data exposure, missing rate limiting and mass assignment. Business logic flaws abuse the intended workflow - like applying a discount code twice or buying a negative quantity - and scanners rarely find them.
lessons.detailed:
OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) highlights: API1 Broken Object Level Authorization; API2 Broken Authentication; API3 Broken Object Property Level Authorization (excessive exposure + mass assignment); API4 Unrestricted Resource Consumption (rate limits); API5 Broken Function Level Authorization; API6 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows; API7 SSRF; API8 Security Misconfiguration; API9 Improper Inventory Management (old v1 endpoints); API10 Unsafe Consumption of APIs.

Testing approach (lab): obtain documentation (OpenAPI/Swagger) -> map endpoints and roles -> test each endpoint with each role -> change IDs (BOLA) -> add unexpected JSON fields like "role":"admin" (mass assignment) -> check responses for extra fields -> send repeated requests to check rate limits (lab only, small volumes) -> test old versions.

Business logic examples: negative quantities, skipping workflow steps (paying after shipping), race conditions on gift cards, unlimited coupon reuse.

Secure API design: authenticate every call (OAuth 2.0/OIDC), authorise per object and function, return only needed fields (response schemas), validate input schemas, rate limit and set quotas, version and retire old APIs, log and monitor.
lessons.analogy: An API is a vending machine for data; BOLA is pressing someone else's button number and getting their snack; mass assignment is slipping in a request for 'free' and the machine obeying.
lessons.example: A fitness app API returned every field of a user object, including private location data, though the app only displayed a name - excessive data exposure.
lessons.relevance: API testing is a fast-growing specialty and features heavily in modern penetration tests and bug bounty programmes.

lessons.summary: Test every endpoint for every role; watch for BOLA, excessive data, mass assignment, rate limits and logic abuse.
lessons.examTip: BOLA is the number one API risk in the OWASP API Top 10 (2023).

lessons.title: Web Testing Tools and Methodology: Burp Suite, OWASP ZAP, DevTools and OWASP WSTG
lessons.why: Tools amplify methodology; methodology ensures coverage.
objectives: Describe intercepting proxies
Use browser devtools and API clients
Follow the OWASP Web Security Testing Guide structure
lessons.simple: An intercepting proxy sits between your browser and the target so you can see and modify every request. Burp Suite (free Community Edition; paid Professional) and OWASP ZAP (free, open source) are the standard tools. Browser developer tools show the DOM, network requests, storage and console. API clients like Postman or the open-source Bruno and Insomnia send crafted API requests. The OWASP Web Security Testing Guide (WSTG) gives a checklist so no area is missed.
lessons.detailed:
Burp Suite components: Proxy (intercept/history), Repeater (resend and modify single requests), Intruder (automated variations - rate-limited in Community), Decoder, Comparer, Target site map. Pro adds the Scanner. ZAP offers Proxy, Spider/AJAX Spider, Active/Passive Scan, Fuzzer, and automation via scripts and Docker.

Set-up (lab): configure the browser to use 127.0.0.1:8080, install the tool's CA certificate in a separate testing browser profile only, set scope to the lab domain so out-of-scope traffic is not recorded.

WSTG categories: Information Gathering, Configuration & Deployment, Identity Management, Authentication, Authorization, Session Management, Input Validation, Error Handling, Cryptography, Business Logic, Client-side, API testing.

Methodology: map the app (all features, roles, endpoints) -> test configuration -> authentication -> session -> authorisation -> input handling -> logic -> client-side -> report. Keep a test log; capture request/response evidence; remove sensitive data before reporting.

Practice platforms: PortSwigger Web Security Academy (free labs), OWASP Juice Shop (run locally), DVWA, TryHackMe/Hack The Box web rooms.
lessons.analogy: Burp Repeater is a rehearsal room where you replay one line of dialogue with tiny changes to see how the actor reacts.
lessons.example: Testers using a structured WSTG checklist found a password-reset logic flaw that an automated scan had missed entirely.
lessons.relevance: Every professional web test uses a proxy and a methodology. BSCP is Burp-focused.

lessons.title: Penetration Testing Methodology and Rules of Engagement
lessons.why: Methodology makes testing safe, legal, repeatable and defensible.
objectives: Describe the phases of a penetration test
Compare common methodologies
Plan an engagement within rules of engagement
lessons.simple: A penetration test is an authorised, time-boxed simulated attack to find and demonstrate security weaknesses so they can be fixed. Common phases are: pre-engagement (scope, rules, authorisation), reconnaissance, scanning and enumeration, vulnerability analysis, controlled exploitation/validation, post-exploitation analysis, reporting and retesting. Methodologies such as PTES, NIST SP 800-115 and the OSSTMM give structure.
lessons.detailed:
Pre-engagement: statement of work, scope (IPs, domains, apps, accounts), exclusions, testing windows, permitted techniques, data handling, communication plan, emergency contacts, stop conditions, legal authorisation letter.

Test types: black box (no info), grey box (some info/credentials), white box (full info, code); external vs internal; network, web, wireless, social engineering, physical (each separately authorised).

Pen test vs vulnerability assessment: the assessment lists weaknesses; the pen test validates and demonstrates impact and chains.
Pen test vs red team: red teams emulate a specific adversary with stealth objectives over longer periods and test detection and response; pen tests aim for breadth of findings.

During testing: keep a timestamped activity log (which IP, what, when) so the client can correlate with their monitoring; pause on instability; report critical issues immediately if agreed.
lessons.analogy: A penetration test is a fire drill with a professional inspector: agreed date, agreed rooms, safety rules, and a report afterwards.
lessons.example: A testing team's activity log let the client's SOC confirm that suspicious traffic at 14:02 was the tester - and that a separate alert at 03:00 was a real intruder.
lessons.relevance: Methodology and RoE compliance are graded in the capstone and expected in every professional role.

lessons.summary: Agree scope and rules first, follow phased methodology, log activity, report and retest.
lessons.examTip: Know the difference between a vulnerability assessment, a penetration test and a red team exercise.

lessons.title: Network, Service, Linux and Windows Security Assessment
lessons.why: Most internal compromises begin with ordinary misconfigurations, not exotic exploits.
objectives: Assess common network services for misconfiguration
Apply Linux and Windows assessment checklists
Relate findings to network architecture and segmentation
lessons.simple: Assessing systems means checking services, configuration and patch levels against good practice. Network services often have weak settings: SMB without signing, anonymous FTP, SNMP with default community strings, exposed databases or management interfaces. Linux checks include SSH configuration, sudo rules, SUID files and services. Windows checks include patch level, local admins, SMB settings, firewall and credential protections. Results are mapped back to the network architecture to see how far an attacker could move.
lessons.detailed:
Service checklist (lab):
• SMB (445): signing required? SMBv1 disabled? anonymous/guest shares?
• FTP (21): anonymous login? cleartext?
• SNMP (161/udp): default 'public'/'private' communities? v3 used?
• RDP (3389): NLA enabled? exposed beyond management networks?
• Databases (1433/3306/5432/27017): listening on all interfaces? default accounts?
• Management (SSH/Telnet/web admin of switches, iLO/iDRAC): default credentials? exposed to user VLANs?

Linux: kernel and package patch level, sshd_config, sudo -l, SUID/SGID, world-writable files, cron scripts, services listening, stored credentials in config files.

Windows: missing patches (Get-HotFix), local admin membership, LAPS, SMB signing, LLMNR/NBT-NS enabled, Credential Guard, AV/EDR status, unquoted service paths, weak service permissions, AlwaysInstallElevated policy.

Network architecture: flat vs segmented, management network isolation, firewall rules between zones, egress filtering.

Tools for evidence: Nmap NSE safe scripts, Netcat banners, configuration reviews with credentials (agreed in scope).
lessons.analogy: Assessment is a building inspection: check each lock, window and fire door against the safety code, then check whether the corridors let fire spread.
lessons.example: An internal test found SNMP 'public' on core switches exposing full configuration - including network diagrams and hashed passwords.
lessons.relevance: These checks generate the majority of real internal pen test findings.

lessons.title: Active Directory, Identity, Authentication Protocols and Credential Protection
lessons.why: Identity is the new perimeter; in most internal tests, AD is the route to full compromise.
objectives: Explain Kerberos and NTLM at assessment level
Identify common AD identity risks
Recommend credential protection controls
lessons.simple: In a Windows domain, users prove who they are to domain controllers using Kerberos (ticket-based) or the older NTLM (challenge-response). Attackers target weaknesses in these processes and in how credentials are stored on machines. Common AD risks include too many privileged accounts, service accounts with weak passwords, legacy protocols and admins logging in to ordinary workstations where their credentials can be stolen. Defences include tiered administration, Credential Guard, LAPS, strong service account management and monitoring.
lessons.detailed:
Kerberos (simplified): user requests a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) from the KDC on the domain controller -> uses the TGT to request service tickets (TGS) -> presents the service ticket to the server. Tickets are encrypted with account-derived keys.

Assessment-level risk concepts (defensive framing):
• Service accounts with SPNs and weak passwords - service tickets can be cracked offline (Kerberoasting). Defence: long random passwords, gMSAs, AES-only.
• Accounts without Kerberos pre-authentication (AS-REP roasting). Defence: require pre-auth.
• NTLM relay where SMB/LDAP signing is not enforced. Defence: enforce signing, disable NTLM where possible, EPA.
• Credentials cached in memory (LSASS) on machines where admins log in. Defence: Credential Guard, LSA protection, tiering, Protected Users group.
• Excessive delegation, dangerous ACLs (GenericAll/WriteDACL on privileged objects), stale admin accounts.

Tools for authorised defensive assessment: BloodHound (graph of AD attack paths - widely used by both red and blue teams), PingCastle (free AD health report), PowerShell AD module.

Detection: event IDs 4768/4769 (Kerberos tickets, watch RC4 requests), 4624 logon type 3/10, 4672, unusual admin logons.
lessons.analogy: Kerberos is a festival wristband system: the main gate (DC) gives you a wristband (TGT), which you show at each tent (service) to get a tent pass (service ticket).
lessons.example: A PingCastle report showed 42 Domain Admins and a service account with a 2014 password; reducing both removed the main attack paths found in the following pen test.
lessons.relevance: AD assessment skills are heavily tested in PNPT and OSCP-style exams and are central to internal pen tests.

lessons.title: Password Security Auditing and Privilege Escalation Concepts
lessons.why: Weak passwords and local misconfigurations turn a foothold into full control.
objectives: Explain offline vs online password auditing and its ethics
Describe John the Ripper, Hashcat and Hydra at concept level
Explain common Linux and Windows privilege escalation paths and fixes
lessons.simple: Password auditing checks whether passwords are strong enough. Online auditing tries passwords against a live login (Hydra is a known tool) - this can lock accounts and must be tightly controlled. Offline auditing tests password hashes obtained in an authorised engagement against wordlists and rules (John the Ripper, Hashcat). Privilege escalation means going from a normal user to administrator or root by abusing misconfigurations or vulnerabilities. You will study the categories and, crucially, how to detect and fix them.
lessons.detailed:
Password auditing rules: written approval for each technique; agree lockout thresholds; never test real users' online logins without explicit permission; handle hashes and cracked passwords as highly sensitive (encrypt, never put plaintext in reports - report counts and patterns); delete at engagement end.

Hash types and speed: NTLM and unsalted MD5/SHA-1 are fast to test; bcrypt/Argon2 are deliberately slow - which is why they are recommended.

Concept-level tools: John the Ripper (format auto-detection, wordlist + rules), Hashcat (GPU-accelerated, mode numbers per hash type), Hydra (online, many protocols - throttled and scoped). In this app's lab you analyse simulated output only.

Linux privilege escalation categories: sudo misconfigurations, SUID binaries, writable cron/scripts run by root, PATH abuse, kernel vulnerabilities, credentials in files, capabilities, container breakouts.
Windows categories: unquoted service paths, weak service/file permissions, AlwaysInstallElevated, stored credentials, token privileges (SeImpersonate), missing patches, scheduled tasks.

Detection and fixes: least privilege, patching, file permission audits, LAPS, removing stored credentials, monitoring new admin group members (4732), sudo logging, EDR alerts.
lessons.analogy: Offline cracking is trying keys on a copied lock at home (no alarms); online guessing is trying keys on the real door while the alarm counts attempts.
lessons.example: An authorised audit found 31% of domain passwords matched a common wordlist plus the year. The client introduced a banned-password list and passphrase guidance.
lessons.relevance: Password auditing results drive identity improvements; privilege escalation knowledge underpins both offensive certifications and system hardening.

lessons.title: Lateral Movement, Segmentation, Detection, Remediation and Tool Education
lessons.why: Clients need to know how far an attacker could go - and whether they would notice.
objectives: Explain lateral movement concepts and segmentation's role
Describe detection and logging for network attacks
Explain the purpose and limits of Metasploit, Searchsploit and Netcat
lessons.simple: Lateral movement is how an attacker moves from one compromised machine to others, typically by reusing credentials or remote administration features (SMB, RDP, WinRM, SSH). Network segmentation and least privilege limit how far they can go. Detection means logging and alerting on suspicious authentication and remote execution. Metasploit is an exploitation framework used to validate vulnerabilities in controlled conditions; Searchsploit searches a local copy of Exploit-DB; Netcat reads and writes raw network connections.
lessons.detailed:
Lateral movement concepts: credential reuse (same local admin password), remote services (PsExec-style SMB execution, WMI, WinRM, RDP, SSH), pass-the-hash/ticket (using credential material instead of passwords). Defensive mapping: MITRE ATT&CK TA0008.

Segmentation testing: from each zone, check what can be reached (e.g. can the guest VLAN reach the server VLAN on 445?). Document allowed paths vs policy.

Detection: Windows 4624 type 3/10, 4648 (explicit credentials), 7045 (service install), Sysmon event 1 (process creation) and 3 (network); Linux auth logs; network IDS (Suricata, Zeek - free); EDR telemetry. Good tests record which actions were or were not detected - valuable feedback for the blue team.

Tool education (lab only):
• Metasploit Framework (open source): modules (exploit, auxiliary, post), payload choice, check commands to verify vulnerability without exploitation where available. Limits: can crash services; noisy; detected by EDR.
• Searchsploit: offline Exploit-DB search; always review code before running anything - public exploits can be broken or malicious.
• Netcat: banner grabbing, simple port checks, file transfer in labs.

Remediation and verification: fix root causes (patch, harden, unique credentials, segmentation rules), then retest the same paths to prove closure.
lessons.analogy: Lateral movement is a burglar using a stolen master key to open every door; segmentation means each wing needs a different key and there is a guard (monitoring) in each corridor.
lessons.example: Replacing a shared local administrator password with LAPS and enforcing firewall rules between workstation subnets stopped a red team from spreading beyond the first laptop.
lessons.relevance: Reports that explain attack paths and detection gaps give clients the most value.

lessons.summary: Lateral movement relies on credentials and remote services; segmentation and monitoring contain it; tools validate - carefully - and retesting proves fixes.

lessons.title: Wireless Fundamentals: Standards, Bands, Access Points and WPA2/WPA3
lessons.why: Wi-Fi is often the easiest way into a building's network - and a common audit area.
objectives: Describe 802.11 standards and frequency bands
Explain WPA2/WPA3 Personal and Enterprise
Identify secure wireless settings
lessons.simple: Wi-Fi follows IEEE 802.11 standards. Wi-Fi 4 (802.11n), 5 (802.11ac), 6/6E (802.11ax) and 7 (802.11be) offer increasing speeds. They use the 2.4 GHz band (longer range, more interference), 5 GHz (faster, shorter range) and 6 GHz (Wi-Fi 6E/7). An access point broadcasts a network name (SSID). Security protocols protect the connection: WEP and WPA are obsolete and broken; WPA2 is widely used; WPA3 is the current standard with stronger protection against password guessing.
lessons.detailed:
Authentication modes:
• Personal (PSK/SAE): one shared passphrase. WPA2-PSK handshakes can be captured and guessed offline if the passphrase is weak. WPA3-SAE resists offline guessing and gives forward secrecy.
• Enterprise (802.1X/EAP with RADIUS): each user/device authenticates individually (EAP-TLS with certificates is strongest). Misconfigured clients that do not validate the server certificate can be tricked by fake access points.

Encryption: WPA2 uses AES-CCMP; avoid TKIP. WPA3 adds SAE, mandatory PMF (protected management frames - mitigates deauthentication attacks), and 192-bit mode for Enterprise.

Other settings: WPS (PIN-based setup) should be disabled - its PIN design is weak. Hiding the SSID is not security. MAC filtering is easily bypassed. Separate guest networks with client isolation. Strong, long passphrases (20+ characters) for PSK networks.
lessons.analogy: WPA2-Personal is one shared house key everyone copies; WPA2/3-Enterprise gives every resident their own key card that can be cancelled individually.
lessons.example: An office used an 8-character WPA2 passphrase printed on the reception wall; a passphrase change and a move to Enterprise authentication for staff fixed both exposure and guessing risk.
lessons.relevance: Wireless reviews check protocol, authentication mode, passphrase strength, WPS, guest isolation and rogue devices.
practice: Open the Wireless Config Review lab
Rank WEP, WPA, WPA2-PSK, WPA3-SAE, WPA2-Enterprise EAP-TLS by strength
List five secure AP settings
lessons.challenge: Write recommendations for a café that uses one WPA2 password for both staff tills and customers.
mistakes: Thinking a hidden SSID is secure
Leaving WPS enabled
Using TKIP for compatibility
lessons.summary: Prefer WPA3 (or WPA2-AES with long passphrases), Enterprise with certificate validation for staff, no WPS and separate isolated guest networks.
lessons.examTip: WPA3 uses SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) instead of the PSK four-way handshake vulnerable to offline guessing.

quiz.q: Which protocol is current best practice for Wi-Fi security?
Why disable WPS?
options: Its PIN method is weak and can be guessed

quiz.q: Hiding the SSID prevents attackers from finding the network.
quiz.explain: Hidden SSIDs are revealed by client probes; it is not a control.

lessons.title: Wireless Threats, Rogue APs, Bluetooth, IoT and Wireless Defence
lessons.why: Wireless attacks need only proximity, not network access.
objectives: Describe rogue and evil-twin access points
Explain Bluetooth and IoT wireless risks
Apply wireless auditing principles and defences
lessons.simple: Wireless threats include rogue access points (unauthorised APs plugged into the network), evil twins (fake APs copying a legitimate SSID to lure users), deauthentication floods that knock clients offline, weak passphrase guessing and misconfigured Enterprise clients. Bluetooth and IoT devices bring their own short-range wireless risks, often with weak authentication and rare updates. Defences include WPA3, PMF, certificate validation, wireless intrusion detection and regular surveys.
lessons.detailed:
Wireless auditing principles: written authorisation including physical locations and frequencies; never interfere with neighbouring networks; avoid deauthentication unless explicitly agreed (it disrupts service); record channel, BSSID, SSID, encryption and signal for each network; compare against the client's approved AP list to find rogues.

Aircrack-ng suite (concept): airmon-ng (monitor mode), airodump-ng (survey networks and capture handshakes for your own lab AP), aircrack-ng (test passphrase strength against a wordlist). In this app you analyse simulated survey output only.

Bluetooth/BLE: risks include unauthenticated pairing ('Just Works'), outdated stacks, tracking via static addresses. IoT: default credentials, unencrypted protocols, no updates, cloud dependency. Put IoT on isolated VLANs.

Defences: WPA3/PMF, 802.1X with EAP-TLS, certificate validation on clients, WIDS/WIPS, AP inventory, guest isolation, disable unused radios, staff awareness (do not connect to unknown networks), VPN on untrusted Wi-Fi.
lessons.analogy: An evil twin is a fake shop with the same sign as the real one next door - customers walk in and hand over their details without realising.
lessons.example: A wireless survey found an unapproved consumer router under a desk bridging the secure LAN to an open SSID - a rogue AP that bypassed every perimeter control.
lessons.relevance: Rogue APs and weak client configuration are frequent wireless findings.
practice: Use the Wireless lab survey to identify the rogue AP
Recommend defences for a warehouse full of IoT scanners
Explain why deauthentication testing needs explicit approval
lessons.challenge: Write a short wireless security checklist for a small clinic.
mistakes: Capturing traffic of neighbouring networks
Deauthenticating clients without approval
Ignoring Bluetooth and IoT
lessons.summary: Survey with permission, compare against the approved list, and defend with WPA3/PMF, EAP-TLS, WIDS and isolation.
lessons.examTip: PMF (802.11w) protects against deauthentication attacks; it is mandatory in WPA3.

Where should IoT devices be placed?

lessons.title: Android and iOS Architecture, Permissions and Secure Storage
lessons.why: Phones hold email, banking, MFA and corporate data - and their security model differs from desktops.
objectives: Describe Android and iOS security architecture
Explain app sandboxing and permissions
Identify secure and insecure storage
lessons.simple: Android is based on the Linux kernel; each app runs as its own user in a sandbox and must declare permissions. iOS also sandboxes apps, requires code signing and reviews apps in the App Store. Both use hardware-backed key storage (Android Keystore, iOS Secure Enclave/Keychain) and full-device encryption. Apps should store secrets in these secure stores, not in plain files or shared preferences.
lessons.detailed:
Android: Linux kernel + SELinux, app sandbox (unique UID), permissions (normal, dangerous/runtime, special), Play Protect, verified boot, file-based encryption, Keystore (often TEE/StrongBox-backed). Components: activities, services, broadcast receivers, content providers - exported components can be reached by other apps and must be protected.

iOS: Secure Boot chain, code signing, sandbox, entitlements, Data Protection classes, Keychain, Secure Enclave, App Transport Security (enforces HTTPS by default).

Permissions best practice: request the minimum, at the moment needed, explain why; Android 13+ needs runtime notification permission; location 'precise' vs 'approximate'.

Storage review: insecure = plaintext SharedPreferences/NSUserDefaults with tokens, world-readable files, logs containing personal data, unencrypted SQLite with sensitive data, backups including secrets. Secure = Keystore/Keychain for keys, encrypted storage for sensitive data, exclude secrets from backups.

Rooting/jailbreaking removes protections; high-risk apps may detect it (defence in depth, not a guarantee).
lessons.analogy: Each app is a hotel guest in its own locked room (sandbox); permissions are the extra keys reception hands out only when asked and approved; the Keystore is the hotel safe.
lessons.example: A banking app stored a long-lived session token in plaintext app storage; on a rooted test device it could be copied and reused - fixed by moving it to the Keystore and shortening its lifetime.
lessons.relevance: Mobile assessments check permissions, storage, components and network security against OWASP MASVS.
practice: Complete the Mobile Permissions Review lab
Classify five storage locations as secure or insecure
Check the permissions of an app on your own phone
lessons.challenge: A torch app requests contacts and SMS permissions. Write the review finding.
mistakes: Storing tokens in plaintext preferences
Exporting components without permission checks
Requesting all permissions at install time
lessons.summary: Both platforms sandbox apps; request minimal permissions; keep secrets in hardware-backed stores; protect exported components.
lessons.examTip: On Android, each app gets its own Linux user ID - the basis of its sandbox.

quiz.q: Where should an Android app store cryptographic keys?

lessons.title: Mobile Application Testing, APIs, Privacy, MobSF and Hardening
lessons.why: Mobile apps are front ends to APIs; most serious mobile findings are really back-end findings.
objectives: Apply OWASP MASVS and MASTG
Use MobSF for static analysis of sample apps
Recommend mobile app hardening and privacy controls
lessons.simple: Mobile application testing combines static analysis (inspecting the app package without running it), dynamic analysis (watching it run on a test device or emulator) and API testing (the back end it talks to). The OWASP Mobile Application Security Verification Standard (MASVS) defines what to check and the Testing Guide (MASTG) explains how. MobSF (Mobile Security Framework) is a free, open-source tool that automates static and dynamic analysis of Android and iOS apps.
lessons.detailed:
MASVS control groups: STORAGE, CRYPTO, AUTH, NETWORK, PLATFORM, CODE, RESILIENCE, PRIVACY.

Static checks (sample/authorised APK only): manifest (debuggable=true? allowBackup? exported components?), hardcoded secrets and API keys, insecure crypto, cleartext traffic allowed (network security config), third-party SDKs and trackers. Tools: MobSF, jadx (decompiler), apktool.

Dynamic checks (test device/emulator): traffic through a proxy (Burp/ZAP) with a test CA; certificate pinning behaviour; data written to storage and logs; authentication flows; deep links. Android debugging tools: adb (logcat, install, shell), emulator.

API communication: everything from Module 9 applies - BOLA, auth, rate limits. Never trust the app to enforce security.

Privacy: data minimisation, consent, clear privacy policy, no excessive tracking SDKs, GDPR rights.

Hardening: remove debug flags, obfuscate (R8/ProGuard) as defence in depth, certificate pinning where appropriate, root/jailbreak detection for high-risk apps, secure storage, no secrets in the app, Play Integrity / App Attest for API abuse protection.
lessons.analogy: Testing a mobile app is checking both the car (the app) and the roads it drives on (the APIs) - most crashes happen on the road.
lessons.example: MobSF static analysis of a sample app revealed a hardcoded cloud API key that granted write access to a storage bucket - the key was rotated and moved server-side.
lessons.relevance: Mobile testing roles expect MASVS knowledge and familiarity with MobSF, jadx and proxies.
practice: Complete Project 10 (mobile security review) using the sample app report
Map five findings to MASVS groups
Create a mobile security checklist
lessons.challenge: Write remediation for 'android:debuggable=true in release build' and 'cleartext traffic permitted'.
mistakes: Testing apps you do not have permission to analyse
Only testing the app and not its API
Treating obfuscation as a security fix
lessons.summary: Use MASVS/MASTG, static + dynamic + API testing, and recommend secure storage, no embedded secrets and server-side enforcement.
lessons.examTip: Hardcoded secrets in an app are always extractable - the fix is to move them server-side.

options: Extractable by anyone with the app

title: Exploitation & Post-Exploitation Concepts
intro: Exploitation is taught here from a security-understanding and controlled-validation perspective: what makes something exploitable, how professionals prove impact safely, what post-exploitation risk looks like, and how defenders detect, contain and recover. No destructive payloads, real credential theft, stealth or evasion are taught.
objectives: Distinguish vulnerability, exploit and proof of concept
Assess exploitability and impact
Plan controlled validation with safety checks
Explain post-exploitation risks and their indicators
Support detection, containment, cleanup, recovery and responsible disclosure

lessons.title: Exploit Fundamentals: Vulnerability vs Exploit, Proof of Concept and Lifecycle
lessons.why: Understanding exploitability is how you rate risk accurately and explain it convincingly.
objectives: Define exploit, payload and proof of concept
Describe the exploit lifecycle
Assess exploitability factors
lessons.simple: A vulnerability is a weakness; an exploit is a technique or code that uses that weakness to achieve something the system should not allow. A proof of concept (PoC) demonstrates that exploitation is possible, ideally with minimal impact. Exploitability depends on factors such as network reachability, required privileges, user interaction, reliability and available public code. Impact is what an attacker gains: data access, code execution, privilege or disruption.
lessons.detailed:
Exploit classes (conceptual): memory corruption (buffer overflows, use-after-free), injection (SQL, command), logic flaws, authentication bypass, deserialization, misconfiguration abuse.

Components: the exploit (triggers the flaw) and the payload (what runs afterwards). In professional validation, payloads are minimal and benign (e.g. print a version or create a harmless marker file in a lab).

Exploit lifecycle: discovery -> PoC -> weaponisation by criminals (sometimes) -> public release -> inclusion in frameworks -> mass exploitation -> patch adoption. Exploit maturity is reflected in CVSS threat metrics and KEV.

Exploitability assessment questions: Is it reachable from where an attacker would be? Does it need authentication? Is user interaction required? Is the public exploit reliable or likely to crash the service? Are mitigations (ASLR, DEP, WAF, EDR) present?

Mitigations against memory corruption: ASLR, DEP/NX, stack canaries, CFG/CET, memory-safe languages (Rust, Go, managed languages).
lessons.analogy: The vulnerability is a crack in a dam; the exploit is the method that widens it; the proof of concept is showing the engineer a trickle - not flooding the valley.
lessons.example: A public PoC for a critical vulnerability was unreliable and crashed servers; testers who validated with vendor check scripts instead avoided causing an outage.
lessons.relevance: Exploitability judgements change severity, priority and how you advise clients.
practice: Answer the five exploitability questions for two sample findings
Explain three memory corruption mitigations
Read the Exploit Validation safety lab briefing
lessons.challenge: Explain to a manager the difference between 'a PoC exists' and 'attackers are exploiting this in the wild'.
mistakes: Equating 'exploit exists' with 'we must exploit it to prove it'
Ignoring service stability
Using unreviewed public code
lessons.summary: Exploitability = reachability + preconditions + reliability - mitigations. Prove existence minimally; describe impact clearly.
lessons.examTip: A payload is what executes after successful exploitation - in professional validation it should be benign.

quiz.q: What is a proof of concept?
options: A demonstration that a vulnerability can be exploited

quiz.q: Which mitigation randomises memory locations?
Which factor LOWERS exploitability?

lessons.title: Controlled Validation and Safety Checks
lessons.why: The professional standard is: prove it safely, or do not do it.
objectives: Plan controlled validation
Apply pre-validation safety checks
Choose the least impactful evidence
lessons.simple: Controlled validation confirms a vulnerability is real and shows its impact while protecting the client's systems and data. Before validating, check scope and authorisation for that specific technique, the system's fragility, backups or snapshots, timing, and that the client contact is reachable. Prefer non-destructive checks (vendor check scripts, version endpoints, read-only proof) over full exploitation. Stop immediately if anything behaves unexpectedly.
lessons.detailed:
Pre-validation checklist:
1. Is this host and technique explicitly in scope?
2. Is exploitation (not just identification) permitted for this engagement?
3. Is the system production, fragile or safety-critical? (medical, OT, payment)
4. Is there a snapshot/backup and a rollback plan? (always in labs)
5. Is the client contact informed and reachable now?
6. What is the minimal evidence that proves impact?
7. What are the stop conditions?

Evidence ladder (least to most impact): version/configuration evidence -> vendor-provided safe check -> harmless behaviour proof (e.g. an error difference, reading a non-sensitive file such as a hostname in a lab) -> controlled code execution of a benign command (whoami) in authorised scope -> anything beyond requires explicit client agreement.

Data handling: never exfiltrate real personal or sensitive data as proof; screenshot minimal redacted evidence; log every action with timestamps.

Lab practice: restore snapshots after validation, verify integrity, document.
lessons.analogy: Controlled validation is a surgeon's biopsy: take the smallest sample needed to confirm the diagnosis, not remove the organ.
lessons.example: A tester proved database access by showing the database version and the count of rows in a table, rather than downloading customer data. The client accepted the finding as critical.
lessons.relevance: Safety and scope compliance are scored in the capstone; in real life they protect clients and your career.
practice: Complete the Exploit Validation Safety decision lab
Order five evidence types from least to most impactful
Write your personal stop conditions
lessons.challenge: A critical RCE is found on a hospital's patient-monitoring gateway. Write what you do next, step by step.
mistakes: Exploiting fragile production systems to 'be sure'
Downloading real data as proof
Continuing after unexpected behaviour
lessons.summary: Check scope, fragility and rollback; use the least impactful evidence; stop on surprises; restore and document.
lessons.examTip: When unsure whether a technique is in scope, the professional answer is to stop and ask the client.

quiz.q: Which is the least impactful way to validate a vulnerability?
options: Vendor-provided safe check or configuration evidence
quiz.explain: Use the lowest-impact evidence that proves the issue.

quiz.q: During validation the target service slows down dramatically. You should...
options: Stop and contact the client per stop conditions
Restart it yourself without telling anyone

quiz.q: Downloading real customer records is acceptable proof of SQL injection.

lessons.title: Post-Exploitation Risk: Privilege, Lateral Movement, Persistence and Evidence
lessons.why: Clients need to understand what an attacker could do next - and defenders need to know what to look for.
objectives: Explain post-exploitation risk categories
Identify post-exploitation indicators
Collect evidence professionally
lessons.simple: Post-exploitation is what happens after an attacker gains a foothold: escalating privileges, moving to other systems, establishing persistence and accessing data. In professional testing, this phase is about analysing and demonstrating risk within agreed limits - for example showing that a compromised web server could reach the database network - not about hiding or staying in the environment. Defenders study the same stages to detect intrusions early.
lessons.detailed:
Risk categories (MITRE ATT&CK tactics): Privilege Escalation (TA0004), Credential Access (TA0006), Discovery (TA0007), Lateral Movement (TA0008), Collection (TA0009), Persistence (TA0003), Exfiltration (TA0010), Impact (TA0040).

Persistence risks (awareness): new services, scheduled tasks/cron, Run keys, new accounts, web shells, SSH authorized_keys entries, startup items. Professional testers do NOT install persistence unless explicitly agreed, and remove all artefacts.

Indicators of post-exploitation activity: new local admins (4732), new services (7045), unusual scheduled tasks (4698), logons at odd hours from unusual hosts, Office apps spawning shells, encoded PowerShell, new files in web roots, outbound connections to unknown hosts, discovery commands in bulk (whoami, net group, ipconfig).

Evidence collection: timestamps (UTC), host, user context, command/action, output (redacted), screenshot, hash of any file obtained, chain-of-custody notes for anything sensitive. Keep a cleanup list of every artefact you create.
lessons.analogy: Post-exploitation analysis is a fire investigator explaining how far the fire could have spread through open doors - not starting more fires to prove it.
lessons.example: A test demonstrated that the compromised web server's service account could read the HR file share - one screenshot of the directory listing (no file contents) was enough to show impact.
lessons.relevance: Your report's attack narrative and the client's detection improvements both come from this phase.
practice: Map ten indicators to ATT&CK tactics
Complete the Incident Log Analysis lab and find post-exploitation indicators
Write an evidence log entry
lessons.challenge: From a simulated host log, build a timeline of the intruder's post-exploitation steps.
mistakes: Creating persistence without permission
Forgetting to track artefacts for cleanup
Collecting more data than needed
lessons.summary: Analyse and demonstrate post-exploitation risk minimally, know the indicators, and keep evidence and cleanup logs.
lessons.examTip: Know at least five ATT&CK tactic names and their purpose.

quiz.q: Which Windows event ID indicates a member was added to a security-enabled local group?
A new file 'img.php' appears in a web root after an alert. It may be...
quiz.explain: Unexpected scripts in web roots suggest web shells.

quiz.q: Professional testers should create persistence...
options: Only if explicitly agreed, and then remove it

lessons.title: Detection, Containment, Cleanup, Recovery and Responsible Disclosure
lessons.why: The end goal of offensive knowledge is better defence and safe, honest communication.
objectives: Observe how detection tools respond
Plan containment, cleanup and recovery
Follow responsible disclosure
lessons.simple: Detection tools such as EDR, SIEM and IDS should alert on exploitation and post-exploitation behaviour; good tests record what was detected. Containment isolates affected systems to stop spread. Cleanup removes every artefact a tester (or attacker) created. Recovery restores systems to a known good state, verified by integrity checks. Responsible (coordinated) disclosure is how researchers report vulnerabilities to vendors privately and give them time to fix before publishing.
lessons.detailed:
Detection feedback: for each test action record time, technique, expected detection, actual alert (yes/no), time to alert. This turns a pen test into purple-team value.

Containment (incident view): network isolation via EDR, disable compromised accounts, block IOCs, preserve evidence (memory/disk images) before wiping.

Tester cleanup: remove uploaded files, test accounts, scheduled tasks, tools; restore changed configuration; confirm with the client; list any artefacts that could not be removed in the report.

Recovery: rebuild from trusted images or restore lab snapshots; reset credentials; patch; verify integrity with hashes/baselines; monitor closely afterwards.

Responsible disclosure: report privately to the vendor/security.txt contact with clear details; agree a timeline (commonly 90 days); do not access more data than needed; do not threaten or demand payment; follow bug bounty rules (scope, safe harbour); publish after a fix or agreed deadline. CVE IDs are assigned through CNAs. Many countries are updating laws to protect good-faith research - check yours.
lessons.analogy: Cleanup is leaving the client's house exactly as you found it - and listing every drawer you opened.
lessons.example: A researcher who found a flaw in a medical device reported it via the manufacturer's disclosure policy; a patch was released and the researcher was credited in the advisory.
lessons.relevance: Detection feedback, cleanup records and disclosure ethics demonstrate professionalism and are part of capstone scoring.
practice: Restore a lab snapshot and verify integrity with hashes
Fill a detection feedback table for five lab actions
Find a real organisation's security.txt and read its disclosure policy
lessons.challenge: Write a responsible disclosure email to a fictional vendor about an IDOR in their API.
mistakes: Leaving test accounts or files behind
Publishing a zero-day without notifying the vendor
Wiping systems before preserving evidence in an incident
lessons.summary: Measure detection, contain, clean up completely, recover to a verified state and disclose responsibly.
lessons.examTip: A common disclosure window is 90 days - a widely used industry norm, not a law.

quiz.q: What should happen before wiping a compromised system during incident response?
options: Preserve evidence such as memory and disk images

quiz.q: Responsible disclosure means...
options: Privately reporting to the vendor and allowing time to fix

quiz.q: Which file can tell researchers how to report vulnerabilities to a website owner?

title: Advanced Security Testing
intro: Modern environments mean identity platforms, cloud, containers, APIs, source code and compiled binaries. This module builds advanced, defence-aware assessment skills in each area.
objectives: Audit Active Directory with defensive tooling
Assess AWS, Azure and Google Cloud configurations
Review Docker and Kubernetes security

lessons.title: Active Directory Security: Architecture, Misconfigurations, Auditing and Hardening
lessons.why: AD compromise usually means total organisational compromise.
objectives: Describe AD architecture in depth
Identify common AD misconfigurations
Audit and harden AD with free tools
lessons.simple: Active Directory consists of domains, forests and trusts, with domain controllers hosting the directory, Kerberos and DNS. Security depends on who has privileged rights (directly or via nested groups and object permissions), how authentication protocols are configured and how Group Policy is managed. Free tools like PingCastle and BloodHound Community Edition reveal risky configurations and attack paths so they can be fixed.
lessons.detailed:
Architecture: forest (security boundary), domains, OUs, sites, trusts (direction, transitivity, SID filtering), FSMO roles, LDAP (389/636), Kerberos (88), global catalog (3268).

Common misconfigurations: excessive Domain/Enterprise Admins; nested groups granting hidden privilege; dangerous ACEs (GenericAll, WriteDACL, WriteOwner on users/groups/GPOs); unconstrained delegation; old OS domain controllers; LDAP signing/channel binding not enforced; NTLMv1 allowed; passwords in GPP/SYSVOL scripts; stale accounts; krbtgt password never rotated; AdminSDHolder misuse; weak service account passwords.

Defensive auditing: PingCastle health check (score + recommendations), BloodHound CE (shortest paths to Domain Admins), Purple Knight (free), PowerShell AD module queries (Get-ADUser -Filter {PasswordNeverExpires -eq $true}).

Hardening: tiered admin model (Tier 0 = DCs and identity), Privileged Access Workstations, Protected Users group, LAPS, disable NTLM where possible, enforce LDAP signing, rotate krbtgt twice per schedule, gMSAs, audit policy + monitoring (4728/4732/4756 group changes, 5136 directory changes), Microsoft Defender for Identity or free alternatives.
lessons.analogy: AD privileges are like building access badges that can be copied through relationships: if the cleaner's badge can open the manager's office where spare master keys are kept, the cleaner effectively has a master key.
lessons.example: BloodHound showed that a help-desk group had WriteDACL over a group nested in Domain Admins - a three-step path to full domain control that nobody knew about.
lessons.relevance: Internal tests and red teams focus on AD; defenders use the same graphs to cut attack paths.

List ten AD hardening controls by impact

lessons.summary: Find privilege through groups and ACLs, check protocol settings, and harden with tiering, LAPS, signing and monitoring.
lessons.examTip: The forest, not the domain, is the security boundary in AD.

lessons.title: Cloud Security: AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, IAM, Storage, Logging and Threat Modelling
lessons.why: Most new infrastructure is in the cloud, and most cloud breaches are misconfigurations.
objectives: Apply the shared responsibility model
Assess IAM, storage and network configuration
Use cloud logging and threat modelling
lessons.simple: In the cloud, the provider secures the physical infrastructure and core services; the customer secures identities, configurations, data and workloads. Identity and Access Management (IAM) is the cloud's main security control - overly broad permissions are the most common serious issue. Other frequent problems are public storage buckets, open security groups, missing logging and leaked access keys. Cloud testing must follow each provider's penetration testing policy.
lessons.detailed:
Provider concepts:
• AWS: IAM users/roles/policies, S3 buckets, EC2 + security groups, VPC, CloudTrail (API logs), GuardDuty, Config, IMDSv2.
• Azure: Entra ID (identities), RBAC roles, subscriptions/resource groups, Storage accounts/Blob, NSGs, Activity Log, Defender for Cloud.
• Google Cloud: IAM with roles on projects/folders/organisation, Cloud Storage, VPC firewall rules, Cloud Audit Logs, Security Command Center.

Common misconfigurations: wildcard policies ("Action": "*", "Resource": "*"); long-lived access keys for humans; no MFA on root/global admins; public buckets/blobs; security groups allowing 0.0.0.0/0 to SSH/RDP/databases; disabled or short-retention logging; unencrypted snapshots shared publicly; IMDSv1 enabled; secrets in environment variables or code.

Assessment approach: review with read-only credentials (e.g. SecurityAudit/Reader roles); free tools - Prowler (AWS/Azure/GCP), ScoutSuite, CloudSploit, Steampipe; map to CIS Foundations Benchmarks.

Cloud threat modelling: identify assets, trust boundaries (internet -> load balancer -> compute -> data), identities and their permissions, data flows; ask STRIDE questions; prioritise identity and data exposure.

Pen testing policy: AWS and Azure and GCP allow testing of your own resources for most services without pre-approval but prohibit DoS and testing the provider's infrastructure - always check current policy.
lessons.analogy: The cloud provider builds and guards the apartment block; you choose who gets keys to your flat and whether you leave the windows open.
lessons.example: A public storage bucket containing database backups was found by automated scanning bots within hours of being made public.
lessons.relevance: Cloud security engineers and testers review IAM and configuration far more than they exploit software bugs.

lessons.summary: Customers own identity and configuration. Audit IAM, storage, network and logging read-only against CIS benchmarks, within provider policy.

lessons.title: Container Security: Docker, Images, Registries, Secrets and Kubernetes
lessons.why: Containers run much of today's software; misconfiguration can expose the host.
objectives: Explain container architecture and isolation
Review images, registries and secrets handling
Identify Kubernetes security basics and hardening
lessons.simple: A container packages an application with its dependencies and runs it isolated using Linux kernel features (namespaces and cgroups). Images are built from Dockerfiles and stored in registries. Because containers share the host kernel, dangerous settings - running as root, --privileged mode, mounting the Docker socket - can let a compromised container affect the host. Kubernetes orchestrates many containers and adds its own security controls such as RBAC, network policies and pod security standards.
lessons.detailed:
Docker review checklist:
• Image: minimal base (distroless/alpine/slim), pinned versions, no secrets baked in (check layers with 'docker history'), scanned with Trivy or Grype (free).
• Runtime: run as non-root (USER in Dockerfile), no --privileged, drop capabilities, read-only filesystem, no /var/run/docker.sock mount, resource limits, seccomp/AppArmor profiles.
• Secrets: use Docker/Kubernetes secrets or an external vault, not ENV variables in images.
• Registries: private, authenticated, image signing (cosign/Notary), vulnerability scanning on push.
• Networking: only publish needed ports; separate networks per app.

Kubernetes basics: API server (protect it - not public), etcd (encrypt, restrict), kubelet (authN/authZ on), RBAC least privilege (avoid cluster-admin for apps), service accounts (disable automount when unused), NetworkPolicies (default deny), Pod Security Standards (restricted), audit logging, namespaces for separation. Free tools: kube-bench (CIS benchmark), kubescape, Trivy.

Image vulnerability assessment: scan, prioritise by fixable/critical/reachable, rebuild regularly, avoid 'latest' tags.
lessons.analogy: Containers are tents on the same campsite sharing one ground (the kernel); a privileged container is a tent with a trapdoor into the campsite office.
lessons.example: A cryptomining campaign targeted Kubernetes dashboards exposed to the internet without authentication.
lessons.relevance: Container and Kubernetes reviews are growing parts of cloud and DevSecOps roles.

List five Kubernetes hardening controls
lessons.challenge: Explain why mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a container is equivalent to giving it root on the host.
mistakes: Using 'latest' tags in production
Storing secrets in image layers
Running everything as root with --privileged
lessons.summary: Minimal, scanned, signed images; non-root, unprivileged runtime; real secrets management; Kubernetes RBAC, network policies and pod security.
lessons.examTip: Namespaces isolate what a container can see; cgroups limit what resources it can use.

lessons.title: API Security: Architecture, Tokens, Authorisation, Discovery and Hardening
lessons.why: APIs carry most modern data flows, and token mistakes are subtle and severe.
objectives: Assess API authentication and token handling
Discover undocumented and shadow APIs
Harden APIs end to end
lessons.simple: API security builds on Module 9. Most APIs use tokens: API keys for applications, OAuth 2.0 access tokens and OpenID Connect ID tokens for users, often as JWTs. Security depends on correctly validating tokens, scoping them, expiring them and authorising every object and function. Discovery finds every API an organisation exposes, including forgotten versions and shadow APIs nobody documented.
lessons.detailed:
Token security: JWT signature verified with the right algorithm (reject 'none', avoid algorithm confusion between RS256/HS256), check exp/iss/aud, short lifetimes with refresh tokens, store securely (HttpOnly cookies or secure platform storage), revoke on logout/compromise. OAuth: use Authorization Code + PKCE for public clients; avoid the Implicit flow; validate redirect URIs exactly; least-privilege scopes.

Authorisation: object-level (BOLA), property-level (excessive data, mass assignment), function-level (admin endpoints) - test every role on every endpoint.

Rate limiting and resource consumption: per user/IP/token limits, pagination caps, payload size limits, timeouts; GraphQL depth and complexity limits; disable introspection in production if not needed.

Data validation: JSON schema validation, type and range checks, reject unknown fields.

API discovery: OpenAPI files, JavaScript bundles, mobile apps, gateway inventories, certificate logs, traffic analysis - all within scope. Old versions (/v1 still live after /v3) are classic findings (OWASP API9).

Hardening: API gateway (authN, rate limits, schema validation, logging), mTLS for service-to-service, central authorisation, inventory and lifecycle management, monitoring for anomalous usage.
lessons.analogy: A token is a festival wristband: it must be genuine (signature), for the right festival (audience), not expired, and only valid for the areas printed on it (scopes).
lessons.example: An API accepted JWTs with 'alg: none', letting anyone forge an admin token - fixed by enforcing the expected algorithm and key.
lessons.relevance: API security testing is one of the fastest-growing specialties and a core AppSec engineer skill.
practice: Complete Project 8 using the mock API
Write a JWT validation checklist
Build an authorisation test matrix (roles x endpoints)
lessons.challenge: Write a finding for 'deprecated /v1 API still live and missing authorisation checks'.
mistakes: Trusting token claims without verifying the signature
Long-lived tokens with no revocation
Forgetting old API versions
lessons.summary: Validate tokens strictly, authorise every object/property/function, limit resources, validate schemas and inventory every API.
lessons.examTip: For mobile and single-page apps, the recommended OAuth flow is Authorization Code with PKCE.

lessons.title: Source Code Security, Static Analysis and Software Supply Chain
lessons.why: Finding flaws in code is cheaper than finding them in production - and supply chain attacks bypass perimeter defences.
objectives: Perform focused secure code review
Use SAST, dependency and secrets scanning
Explain software supply chain risks and controls
lessons.simple: Secure code review reads source code to find vulnerabilities before release. Static analysis (SAST) tools scan code automatically for risky patterns. Dependency scanning (SCA) finds known-vulnerable libraries, and secrets scanning finds passwords and keys committed to repositories. The software supply chain includes every library, build tool and pipeline step; attackers increasingly compromise these to reach many victims at once.
lessons.detailed:
Manual review focus: sources (user input) -> sinks (SQL queries, OS commands, file paths, HTML output, deserialization, redirects); authentication and authorisation checks; crypto usage; error handling and logging; secrets.

Common weaknesses (CWE Top 25 examples): CWE-79 XSS, CWE-89 SQLi, CWE-78 OS command injection, CWE-22 path traversal, CWE-787 out-of-bounds write, CWE-862 missing authorisation, CWE-798 hardcoded credentials, CWE-502 deserialization.

Free tools: Semgrep (SAST rules), Bandit (Python), SpotBugs/FindSecBugs (Java), ESLint security plugins; SCA - OWASP Dependency-Check, GitHub Dependabot, npm audit, pip-audit, Trivy; secrets - gitleaks, trufflehog; GitHub secret scanning and code scanning (CodeQL) on public repos.

Supply chain: typosquatted packages, compromised maintainer accounts, malicious updates, poisoned build pipelines. Controls: pin and verify dependencies (lockfiles, hashes), SBOMs (CycloneDX/SPDX), signed artefacts (Sigstore/cosign), SLSA build levels, least-privilege CI tokens, branch protection, code review requirements, reproducible builds.

Process: shift-left (scan in IDE and pull requests), triage findings (many SAST results are false positives), fix and add tests.
lessons.analogy: SAST is a spell-checker for security mistakes; SCA checks the ingredients list for recalled products; supply chain security makes sure nobody swapped ingredients at the factory.
lessons.example: A popular open-source compression library had a backdoor inserted by a maintainer over a long period; it was caught shortly before reaching major stable Linux releases - a wake-up call for supply chain verification.
lessons.relevance: Code review and supply chain security are central to AppSec and DevSecOps careers.

lessons.summary: Review sources to sinks, automate SAST/SCA/secrets scanning, and protect the supply chain with pinning, SBOMs and signed builds.
lessons.examTip: A secret committed to Git must be rotated even after removal, because history preserves it.

lessons.title: Binary Analysis, Reverse Engineering and Malware Analysis Foundations
lessons.why: Understanding compiled code lets you verify software integrity, analyse suspicious files and understand memory-safety flaws.
objectives: Describe binaries, assembly and CPU basics
Compare static and dynamic analysis
Apply safe malware analysis foundations
lessons.simple: A binary is a compiled program the CPU runs directly. Reverse engineering works out what a binary does without its source code, using disassemblers and decompilers to turn machine code back into readable form, and debuggers to watch it run. Malware analysis applies these techniques to suspicious files to understand their behaviour and produce detections. It must be done in an isolated lab with no connection to real networks.
lessons.detailed:
Binary fundamentals: formats PE (Windows), ELF (Linux), Mach-O (macOS); sections (.text code, .data, .rdata), imports/exports, entry point; strings; packers.

Assembly introduction (x86-64): registers (RAX, RBX, RCX, RDX, RSP stack pointer, RIP instruction pointer), instructions (mov, add, sub, cmp, jmp, je/jne, call, ret, push, pop), the stack and calling conventions. ARM64 for mobile/Apple.

Static analysis: file type and hashes (sha256sum), strings, imports (what APIs it uses), entropy (packing), disassembly/decompilation. Free tools: Ghidra (NSA, open source), Cutter/radare2, Detect It Easy, PE-bear, YARA for pattern rules.

Dynamic analysis: run in an isolated VM snapshot with no network (or a simulated network such as INetSim/FakeNet-NG), monitor processes (Procmon, Process Explorer), file and registry changes (Regshot), network (Wireshark), debuggers (x64dbg, GDB). Revert the snapshot afterwards.

Malware analysis foundations: triage (hash lookup in threat intel), static, behavioural, code-level; output IOCs (hashes, domains, mutexes, registry keys) and YARA/Sigma detections. Safety: use dedicated analysis VMs, never on your host, disable shared folders/clipboard, handle samples in password-protected archives ('infected' is the convention), comply with law and policy.

Software integrity: verify signatures (Authenticode, GPG), compare hashes, check build provenance.
lessons.analogy: Reverse engineering is taking apart a cake to work out the recipe; dynamic analysis is watching the baker in a sealed kitchen.
lessons.example: Analysts reverse-engineered a ransomware sample in an isolated lab, found a flaw in its key handling and helped victims recover files without paying.
lessons.relevance: These foundations lead to malware analyst, threat researcher and exploit-development careers and improve understanding of memory-safety vulnerabilities.

mistakes: Analysing malware on your everyday computer

lessons.summary: Know binary formats and assembly basics; combine static and dynamic analysis in an isolated lab; produce IOCs and detections; verify software integrity.
lessons.examTip: RIP holds the address of the next instruction on x86-64; controlling it is the goal of many memory-corruption exploits.

title: Reporting & Professional Practice
intro: The report is the product. Clients rarely see your testing - they read your report. This module teaches professional conduct and how to write clear, accurate, actionable penetration testing reports using the in-app Report Builder.
objectives: Operate within ethics, law, authorisation and scope
Communicate with clients professionally
