lessons.title: Professional Ethics, Authorisation, Scope, Boundaries and Client Communication
lessons.why: Trust is the ethical hacker's licence to operate.
objectives: Apply professional ethics in practice
Manage scope changes and boundaries
Communicate clearly with clients before, during and after testing
lessons.simple: Professional practice means behaving so that clients can trust you with access to their most sensitive systems. You work only within written authorisation and scope, respect testing boundaries, communicate promptly about critical issues or incidents, and keep everything confidential. If something unexpected happens - a system crashes, you find evidence of a real attacker, or you are unsure whether something is in scope - you stop and talk to the client.
lessons.detailed:
Authorisation chain: the signatory must have authority over the systems (and third-party hosting may need its own approval). Keep the signed authorisation accessible during testing.

Scope management: any request to add targets mid-test needs written amendment. Discovered assets outside scope are reported as observations, not tested.

Boundaries: testing windows, prohibited techniques (DoS, social engineering, physical), data limits, rate limits.

Communication plan: kick-off meeting (objectives, contacts, logistics), daily or milestone status updates if agreed, immediate notification of critical findings and of any signs of real compromise (pre-existing breach), wrap-up meeting, report delivery through a secure channel, debrief/readout.

Professional conduct: honesty about what was and was not tested, no exaggeration of findings, no disparaging the client's staff, conflicts of interest declared, continuous learning. Codes of ethics: (ISC)2, EC-Council, CREST and many employers have them.
lessons.analogy: Testers are like trusted locksmiths given a client's keys: their reputation depends entirely on doing exactly what was agreed and nothing more.
lessons.example: During an external test a team noticed signs of a real intruder's web shell. They stopped, called the emergency contact and helped the client's incident response - preserving trust and evidence.
lessons.relevance: Professionalism and communication are scored in the capstone executive presentation.
practice: Write a kick-off meeting agenda
Draft a critical-finding notification email
List what you do if you find evidence of a real attacker
lessons.challenge: A client's IT manager verbally asks you to 'also have a quick look' at the HR system. Write your professional response.
mistakes: Accepting scope changes verbally
Waiting until the report to mention a critical issue
Overstating findings to look impressive
lessons.summary: Stay within written scope, communicate early and honestly, stop when unsure and protect confidentiality.
lessons.examTip: If you find signs of an existing compromise, stop and notify the client's emergency contact immediately.

quiz.q: When should a critical finding be communicated?

lessons.title: Evidence Handling, Confidentiality and Data Protection
lessons.why: Your evidence is sensitive client data. Mishandling it can cause the very breach you were hired to prevent.
objectives: Collect sufficient, minimal evidence
Protect evidence in storage and transit
Apply data protection principles to testing data
lessons.simple: Evidence proves your findings: screenshots, request/response pairs, command output and logs. It must be accurate, timestamped and minimal - enough to prove the issue, not more. Store it encrypted, share it only through secure channels and delete it when the contract says. Personal data you encounter is protected by data protection law, so redact it in reports and never keep it longer than necessary.
lessons.detailed:
Good evidence: shows the target (host/URL), the action, the result and the time; is cropped to the relevant part; has sensitive values redacted (show 'password: ********' or the first characters of a hash only); has a caption explaining what it shows; can be reproduced by the client.

Storage: encrypted disks/containers (BitLocker, LUKS, VeraCrypt), separate per client, access-controlled, no personal cloud storage, no evidence on unencrypted USB sticks.

Transmission: encrypted portals or encrypted archives with passwords sent via a different channel; never plain email attachments for full reports with sensitive data.

Retention: follow the contract (e.g. delete raw data 30-90 days after acceptance); keep a deletion record.

GDPR principles applied: lawfulness, purpose limitation (only for the test), data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity and confidentiality, accountability. Report personal data exposure as a finding without copying the data itself.
lessons.analogy: Evidence is a forensic sample: labelled, sealed, stored safely and only as large as needed for the test.
lessons.example: A consultancy lost an unencrypted laptop containing client reports; the incident damaged several client relationships. Full-disk encryption would have made it a non-event.
lessons.relevance: Evidence handling and confidentiality are part of every professional contract and certification code of ethics.

List storage and transfer rules
lessons.challenge: Write the evidence-handling section of a statement of work.
mistakes: Unredacted passwords or personal data in reports
Sending reports as plain email attachments

lessons.summary: Capture minimal, captioned, redacted evidence; encrypt it; transfer securely; delete on schedule.
lessons.examTip: Data minimisation and storage limitation are GDPR principles directly relevant to testers.

lessons.title: Report Structure: Executive Summary, Scope, Methodology and Limitations
lessons.why: Executives decide budgets from the first two pages; engineers fix issues from the rest.
objectives: Structure a professional report
Write an executive summary for non-technical readers
Document scope, methodology and limitations
lessons.simple: A penetration testing report usually contains: an executive summary (business-level findings and risk), a technical summary, scope, methodology, limitations, detailed findings, a remediation table and appendices. The executive summary avoids jargon, states overall risk, the most important issues and the top recommendations. The scope, methodology and limitations sections explain exactly what was tested, how and what was not covered.
lessons.detailed:
Executive summary template:
Purpose: 'Silverline Ltd engaged [Firm] to assess its external web portal between 3-7 March 2026.'
Overall posture: 'Overall risk: HIGH. Two issues could allow an internet attacker to access other customers' data.'
Key findings (2-4 bullets, business language).
Positive observations (what was done well - builds trust and balance).
Top recommendations (prioritised, with timeframes).

Technical summary: counts by severity, key attack chains, themes (e.g. access control weaknesses across APIs).

Scope: targets (URLs, IPs, apps, roles/accounts), dates and times, test type (black/grey/white box), exclusions.

Methodology: standards followed (PTES, OWASP WSTG, NIST SP 800-115), phases, tools (by category), severity rating method (CVSS v3.1 / v4.0 plus contextual risk).

Limitations: time-boxed testing, accounts not provided, systems unavailable, rate limits, production constraints, point-in-time nature.

Use the in-app Report Builder: it generates executive and technical summary drafts from your findings, which you then edit.
lessons.analogy: The executive summary is the newspaper headline and first paragraph; the technical sections are the full investigative article.
lessons.example: A board approved funding for an MFA rollout within a week because the executive summary explained, in one paragraph, how a single stolen password could expose all customer records.
lessons.relevance: Report quality is graded in Project 14 and the capstone; it is what employers ask to see in interviews.
practice: Create a new report in the Report Builder for the fictional Silverline engagement

lessons.challenge: Rewrite a jargon-filled executive summary into plain business language.
mistakes: Technical jargon in the executive summary
No limitations section
Missing positive observations
lessons.summary: Structure: executive -> technical -> scope -> methodology -> limitations -> findings -> remediation -> appendices. Write for each audience.
lessons.examTip: Executive summaries should state overall risk and business impact without technical jargon.

quiz.q: Who is the main audience of the executive summary?
quiz.explain: Leaders who decide priorities and budget.

quiz.q: Which section explains what was NOT tested?
Including positive observations in a report is unprofessional.
quiz.explain: Balanced reports note what is done well.

lessons.title: Writing Findings: Severity, CVSS, Evidence, Impact, Reproduction and Remediation
lessons.why: A finding that cannot be understood or reproduced will not be fixed.
objectives: Write complete, consistent findings
Assign severity with CVSS and context
Write specific, verifiable remediation
lessons.simple: Each finding should have a clear title, severity, affected assets, description, evidence, impact, reproduction context, remediation and references. Severity combines a standard score like CVSS with business context. Impact explains what could happen to the organisation. Remediation must be specific and verifiable, and the remediation table summarises all findings with owners and due dates.
lessons.detailed:
Finding template:
Title: Insecure Direct Object Reference in Invoice API
Severity: High (CVSS 3.1: 7.7 AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N) - adjusted for customer financial data
Affected: https://portal.silverline.test/api/invoices/{id}
Description: The API returns invoices without checking that the requesting user owns them.
Evidence: Request by test user 'learner' for /api/invoices/1002 (owned by test user 'bob') returned HTTP 200 with invoice data (redacted screenshot, Appendix B, 2026-03-04 10:42 UTC).
Impact: Any authenticated customer can view other customers' invoices, exposing names, addresses and purchase history - a likely reportable personal data breach.
Reproduction context: authenticated customer session; change the numeric ID.
Remediation: Enforce ownership checks server-side in the invoice controller using the session user ID; return 404 for objects not owned; add automated authorisation tests per role.
Verification: Retest with two test accounts; expect 404 for cross-account IDs.
References: OWASP API1:2023, CWE-639.

Severity scale: Critical / High / Medium / Low / Informational - define it in the methodology. Remediation table columns: ID, finding, severity, owner, recommended action, target date, status.

Reproduction context is written for defenders to verify, not as a step-by-step weapon - describe conditions and evidence rather than publishing a ready-made attack script.
lessons.analogy: A finding is a medical report: diagnosis (title), how serious (severity), test results (evidence), what could happen (impact) and the prescription (remediation).
lessons.example: A client fixed 18 of 20 findings within a month after a tester rewrote vague advice ('improve input validation') as specific, code-level guidance with verification steps.
lessons.relevance: This is the core professional output of the job and is scored in every project rubric.

lessons.examTip: Remediation should be specific enough that a developer knows what to change and how to test it.

lessons.title: Retesting, Verification and Responsible Disclosure
lessons.why: The engagement is only successful when the risks are actually reduced.
objectives: Plan and perform retests
Write retest results
Apply responsible disclosure outside client engagements
lessons.simple: After the client fixes findings, a retest confirms whether each fix works. You repeat the original test conditions and record each finding as Fixed, Partially fixed, Not fixed or Risk accepted. A retest report or appendix shows the updated status. Outside client work - for example in bug bounties or independent research - responsible disclosure governs how you report vulnerabilities to organisations.
lessons.detailed:
Retest process: confirm retest scope (only original findings unless agreed) -> obtain fix details from the client -> reproduce the original conditions -> try reasonable variations (fixes are often partial, e.g. one endpoint fixed but another still vulnerable) -> record evidence -> update status -> report.

Status definitions:
• Fixed - original issue and reasonable variants no longer present.
• Partially fixed - some instances or variants remain.
• Not fixed - issue still present.
• Risk accepted - client formally accepted (documented).
• Mitigated - compensating control reduces risk; root cause remains.

Verification also covers configuration drift: recommend continuous checks so fixed issues do not return.

Responsible disclosure (independent research): stay within published bug bounty scope and rules; access the minimum data; report privately via security.txt, VDP or bounty platform; give reasonable time; do not demand payment outside programmes; coordinate publication.
lessons.analogy: A retest is the follow-up doctor's appointment: check the treatment worked, and that the illness has not simply moved somewhere else.
lessons.example: A retest found an IDOR fixed on /invoices but still present on /invoices/export - a partial fix the client was glad to catch before customers did.
lessons.relevance: Retests close the loop and are part of the capstone's final stages.
practice: Retest your Silverline findings in the Report Builder and set their statuses

lessons.challenge: Write a retest note for a partially fixed XSS finding.
mistakes: Testing only the exact URL from the original finding
Marking 'fixed' without evidence
Retesting outside agreed scope
lessons.summary: Retest with original conditions plus variants, record clear statuses with evidence, and disclose responsibly in independent research.
lessons.examTip: Partial fixes are common - always test variants of the original issue.

quiz.q: A finding fixed on one endpoint but present on another is...
What should a retest normally cover?
options: The original findings within agreed retest scope

quiz.q: You can mark a finding 'fixed' based on the client's word alone.

lessons.title: Your Practice Ecosystem: Home Lab and Practice Platforms
lessons.why: Skills come from deliberate, legal practice. Knowing where to practise safely matters.
objectives: Maintain a safe home lab
Choose suitable practice platforms
Follow platform rules
lessons.simple: Besides the simulated labs in this app, you can practise on your own isolated virtual lab and on legal training platforms. TryHackMe offers guided rooms for beginners; Hack The Box offers more challenging machines and an academy; PortSwigger Web Security Academy offers free web labs; OWASP Juice Shop is a deliberately insecure web app you run locally. Each platform provides targets you are authorised to attack - never use your skills against systems outside them.
lessons.detailed:
Home lab maintenance: keep attacker and target VMs on an internal network, snapshot before each session, update your attacker VM, keep notes per machine, never expose vulnerable VMs to the internet, and power them off when not in use.

Platforms (free tiers exist; features and prices change - check current details):
• TryHackMe - browser-based guided learning paths (e.g. Pre-Security, Jr Penetration Tester, SOC Level 1).
• Hack The Box - Machines, Challenges, Academy modules and certification paths.
• PortSwigger Web Security Academy - free, high-quality web labs that map to BSCP.
• OWASP Juice Shop - run locally via Docker: a modern vulnerable shop with a score board.
• Others: VulnHub (downloadable VMs), OverTheWire (wargames), PicoCTF (beginner CTF), Blue Team Labs Online and CyberDefenders (defensive).

Rules: follow each platform's terms; do not share flags/solutions publicly where prohibited; use VPN connections only as instructed; never pivot from a platform to the internet.
lessons.analogy: Practice platforms are driving schools with closed tracks: you can practise emergency stops safely - but not on the public road.
lessons.example: Many people hired into junior roles cite consistent practice on legal platforms, with public write-ups of retired machines, as key interview evidence.
lessons.relevance: Consistent practice builds the skills assessed in practical certifications like eJPT, PNPT and OSCP.

lessons.title: Lab Methodology: Notes, Checkpoints, Hints and Reflection
lessons.why: How you practise determines how much you learn from each hour.
objectives: Use a consistent lab workflow
Use hints without losing learning
Reflect to convert practice into skill
lessons.simple: Every lab in this app follows the same structure: scenario, objectives, rules, environment, tasks with checkpoints, hints, a knowledge test, reflection questions, a solution explanation and a defensive lesson. Work methodically: read the rules, make a plan, take notes of every command and result, try before using hints, and always finish with the reflection and the defensive lesson - that is where understanding is cemented.
lessons.detailed:
Recommended workflow:
1. Read scenario, rules and objectives - restate the goal in one sentence.
2. Plan your approach (which phases, which tools).
3. Execute one step at a time; record command, output and interpretation in Notes.
4. Stuck for 15-20 minutes? Use the first hint. Hints are graded: nudge -> direction -> near-solution.
5. Check checkpoints - each confirms a milestone.
6. Complete the knowledge test.
7. Answer reflection questions honestly (what worked, what did not, what would you do differently?).
8. Read the defensive lesson: how would a defender prevent or detect what you did?
9. Write a short finding as if for a report.

Scoring in this app: tasks completed, hints used (small deductions), knowledge test score and completion. Replay labs later for spaced repetition.

Note-taking tools (free): the in-app Notes, Obsidian, Joplin, CherryTree - organised per lab with screenshots.
lessons.analogy: Labs without notes are like gym sessions without tracking - you work hard but cannot see progress or repeat what worked.
lessons.example: Candidates who kept structured notes found practical exams far easier because they had a personal, searchable playbook.

lessons.simple: Projects combine several skills into a realistic task - for example auditing a Linux server or assessing a mock API - and produce a deliverable such as a checklist, network map or report. Each project in this app has tasks, a deliverable and a grading rubric. Completed projects are added to your Portfolio automatically, and the final project is the Silverline Enterprise capstone, a full simulated engagement from client briefing to retest.
lessons.detailed:
Rubric dimensions used across projects: Accuracy, Methodology, Safety & scope compliance, Technical reasoning, Evidence quality, Risk classification, Remediation quality, Report quality, Professional communication.

Rubric levels: Excellent (4), Good (3), Developing (2), Insufficient (1). A project passes at an average of 2.5+ with no 'Insufficient' in Safety & scope.

Portfolio-quality deliverables: clear title and objective, scope statement (fictional organisation), method, findings, remediation, lessons learned; screenshots from labs (no real third-party data); consistent formatting. Export from the Portfolio centre as PDF.

Public portfolio tips: GitHub repository with project write-ups and scripts (no secrets, no real targets), a blog for retired-machine write-ups where platform rules allow, a one-page summary for your CV.

Capstone preparation: revise Modules 6-14, practise the Report Builder, review your weak areas in the Progress centre.

lessons.title: Cybersecurity Career Paths and Roles
lessons.why: Knowing the roles helps you choose a direction and target your learning.
objectives: Describe offensive, defensive and engineering roles
Map roles to skills and modules
Plan a realistic entry route
lessons.simple: Cybersecurity has many roles. Offensive roles (ethical hacker, penetration tester, red team operator) find weaknesses. Defensive roles (SOC analyst, blue team analyst, incident responder, digital forensics analyst) detect and respond to attacks. Engineering and architecture roles (security engineer, cloud security engineer, application security engineer, DevSecOps engineer, security architect) build secure systems. Advisory roles (security consultant, vulnerability analyst) assess and guide. Many people enter through IT support, networking or SOC roles.
lessons.detailed:
Role snapshots (skills -> key modules):
• SOC Analyst (entry): logs, SIEM, alert triage, networking -> M2, M3, M5, M7, M12.
• Vulnerability Analyst: scanning, CVSS, prioritisation -> M7, M8.
• Penetration Tester / Ethical Hacker: methodology, web, network, AD, reporting -> M6-M14.
• Red Team Operator (senior): adversary emulation, stealth tradecraft (beyond this course's scope), detection awareness.
• Blue Team / Incident Responder / Digital Forensics: IR lifecycle, forensics, malware triage -> M5, M12, M13.
• Application Security Engineer: secure code, SAST/DAST, threat modelling -> M4, M9, M13.
• Cloud Security Engineer: IAM, cloud config, containers -> M13.
• DevSecOps Engineer: CI/CD security, supply chain -> M4, M13.
• Security Engineer / Architect: design controls, zero trust -> M5, M13.
• Security Consultant: assessments plus communication -> M14.

Entry routes: IT support/helpdesk -> SOC; networking/sysadmin -> security engineer/pen tester; developer -> AppSec. Apprenticeships and graduate schemes exist in many countries; public sector and NHS-type organisations hire security analysts too.
lessons.analogy: Cybersecurity is like a hospital: there are surgeons (pen testers), emergency doctors (incident responders), infection-control teams (security engineers) and administrators who keep everything compliant (GRC).
lessons.example: Many senior penetration testers started on a service desk, moved to a SOC, then specialised after building a lab and earning a practical certification.

lessons.title: Certification Pathways (Informational)
lessons.why: Certifications help pass CV filters and structure learning, but only practical skill sustains a career.
objectives: Compare entry, intermediate and advanced certifications
Distinguish knowledge-based and practical exams
Plan a certification route
lessons.simple: Certifications show employers you have reached a standard. Some are multiple-choice knowledge exams (CompTIA Security+, CEH multiple-choice), others are practical, hands-on exams (eJPT, PNPT, OSCP, Burp Suite Certified Practitioner). This app maps its modules to common certifications for guidance only. Exam formats, prerequisites and prices change, so always check the official provider's website before booking. This app is not affiliated with or endorsed by any certification body.
lessons.detailed:
Overview (verify current details with each provider):
• CompTIA Security+ - foundational security knowledge; multiple-choice and performance-based questions; widely requested in job adverts. Modules 1-8, 14.
• eJPT (INE) - entry-level practical penetration testing exam. Modules 2, 3, 6-10.
• PNPT (TCM Security) - practical external/internal test including AD, plus a written report and debrief. Modules 6-14.
• CEH (EC-Council) - broad ethical hacking knowledge; a separate practical exam exists. Modules 5-13.
• OSCP (OffSec, course PEN-200) - demanding hands-on exam requiring a professional report. Modules 6-14 plus extensive practice.
• Burp Suite Certified Practitioner (PortSwigger) - practical web application exam. Module 9 + PortSwigger Academy.
Other relevant: CompTIA Network+/CySA+/PenTest+, ISC2 CC (entry) and CISSP (senior, experience required), GIAC certifications (GSEC, GPEN, GWAPT, GCIH), cloud provider security certifications (AWS Security Specialty, Microsoft SC-200/AZ-500), CREST CPSA/CRT (UK-recognised for penetration testing).

Route examples: beginner -> Security+ -> eJPT -> PNPT/OSCP; web focus -> PortSwigger Academy -> BSCP; defensive -> Security+ -> CySA+/SC-200 -> GCIH.

The Career Centre shows each certification card with an 'Informational - verify with provider' label and links that open in your browser when you choose.
lessons.analogy: Certifications are like driving test passes: they prove a standard at a moment in time, but your driving record (portfolio and experience) shows what you can do every day.
lessons.example: Candidates with Security+ and a strong lab portfolio often progress to interviews where practical tasks decide the outcome.
lessons.relevance: Mock exams in the Examination Centre help prepare for knowledge-based exams; labs and projects build practical-exam skills.

lessons.title: CV, LinkedIn and Portfolio
lessons.why: Your CV and portfolio get you the interview; make them evidence-based.
objectives: Write a security-focused CV

lessons.simple: A strong cybersecurity CV is short (one to two pages), tailored to the role and full of evidence: skills demonstrated through projects, labs, certifications and work achievements with results. LinkedIn should match your CV, with a clear headline, summary and featured projects. Your portfolio - exported from this app or hosted on GitHub - shows real work such as reports and scripts based on fictional or lab environments.
lessons.detailed:
CV structure: name and contact (no full address needed), headline (e.g. 'Aspiring Penetration Tester | Security+ | Home Lab & 14 Projects'), profile (3-4 lines), key skills (grouped: networking, Linux/Windows, web security, scripting, reporting), experience (achievement bullets: action + tool + result, e.g. 'Automated weekly patch compliance reporting with PowerShell, cutting manual effort by 4 hours/week'), projects (2-4 with one-line outcomes), certifications, education.

Transferable experience counts: IT support (troubleshooting, users, AD), healthcare systems, networking, development.

LinkedIn: professional photo, headline with target role, About section with story and skills, Featured (portfolio PDF, write-ups), skills endorsed, follow and engage with the community, post lab learnings responsibly.

Portfolio: 3-6 best projects; each with objective, scope (fictional), method, key findings, remediation, lessons; capstone report; scripts on GitHub with README; no secrets, no real targets, no active-platform solutions.

The in-app CV Builder generates a formatted PDF from your entries and pulls in completed projects and certificates.
lessons.analogy: A CV is a movie trailer: show the best scenes (achievements) that make the recruiter want to see the whole film (interview).
lessons.example: A career changer from hospital IT support highlighted EPR access-control work, an AD clean-up and home lab projects - and secured a SOC analyst role.
lessons.relevance: Recruiters often filter CVs in seconds; evidence and keywords matter.

lessons.title: Interviews, Practical Simulations, Communication and Career Progression
lessons.why: Interviews test how you think, communicate and behave - not just what you know.
objectives: Answer technical interview questions with structure
Handle practical interview tasks
Plan long-term career progression
lessons.simple: Security interviews usually combine behavioural questions (teamwork, ethics, handling pressure), technical questions (networking, operating systems, web vulnerabilities, incident handling) and sometimes a practical task (analyse logs, review a report, solve a small lab). Use structure: explain your reasoning, say what you would check next and admit what you do not know - then explain how you would find out. Communication, curiosity and ethics are as important as technical depth.
lessons.detailed:
Answer frameworks:
• STAR for behavioural questions: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
• Technical questions: define -> explain how it works -> security relevance -> example -> mitigation. E.g. 'What is XSS?' -> definition, types, impact, fix.
• Scenario questions ('You see 500 failed logins from one IP...'): clarify -> triage -> investigate -> contain -> communicate -> document.

Common technical topics: OSI/TCP handshake, DNS, common ports, HTTP status codes, OWASP Top 10, SQLi vs XSS, hashing vs encryption, Kerberos basics, privilege escalation concepts, incident response phases, CVSS, how you would test a login page, how you would explain a finding to a manager.

Practical simulations: log analysis, PCAP triage, small web app, report critique. The in-app Interview Simulator gives timed questions with model answers.

Professional communication: tailor detail to the audience, be concise, use risk language with managers, be precise with engineers.

Career progression: junior -> mid (independent engagements, mentoring) -> senior (lead tests, scoping, quality review) -> principal/manager/architect. Keep learning: conferences (BSides events are low-cost), communities, research, CPE credits.
lessons.analogy: An interview is a short lab where the target is your reasoning: interviewers want to watch how you approach the problem.
lessons.example: A candidate who said 'I am not sure, but I would check the Security event log for 4625 events and correlate the source IP' impressed more than one who guessed confidently and was wrong.
